stories.Headline: California Closes 2026 Legislative Session With Sweeping New Privacy and AI Laws
stories.Summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom closed out California's 2026 legislative session by signing 22 of the 25 major privacy and artificial intelligence bills that reached him by the September 30 deadline, and vetoing the other three. The signed laws touch the California Consumer Privacy Act, the California Invasion of Privacy Act, data brokers, children's privacy, AI transparency, automated employment decisions, workplace surveillance, health care AI, chatbots, digital replicas and AI auditing. One of the most closely watched is SB 690, which changes how website-tracking lawsuits under the Invasion of Privacy Act are handled. When an alleged violation of the pen-register and trap-and-trace provision, section 638.51, arises from conduct on a website or app, only the state Attorney General may now bring a civil action against a private actor. Before the change, that remedy allowed damages of $5,000 per violation, or three times actual damages if greater, without proof of actual harm.

SB 690 also applies to pending cases, covering claims in actions begun within two years before its January 1, 2027 operative date, meaning actions filed on or after January 1, 2025. Reuters has reported more than 4,700 digital wiretapping suits since 2022, with about two-thirds including a pen-register claim. The law does not end this litigation, because wiretapping claims under sections 631 and 632 remain open to private plaintiffs. Other new requirements include SB 923, which extends the consumer deletion right under the CCPA to data collected "from or about" a person, including data obtained from third parties, and AB 883, which shortens certain 45-day data broker deadlines to 30 days. Data brokers also face the state's deletion platform, DROP, which launched August 1, 2026 and requires more than 500 registered brokers to process centralized deletion and opt-out requests.

The rules on children, chatbots and employment are equally broad. AB 2246 replaces the Age-Appropriate Design Code Act and AB 1709 bars specified addictive features for users under 16, while SB 867 bans toys containing companion chatbots. SB 947 prevents employers from relying solely on an automated decision system for discipline or termination, and AB 1883 restricts AI-enabled workplace surveillance, including neural data collection and emotion recognition. In health care, AB 1979 bars AI from independently performing clinical functions reserved for licensed professionals, and AB 1405 requires the Government Operations Agency to create an AI Auditor Registry. The three vetoed bills were AB 1542 on sensitive personal information, SB 903 on AI in psychotherapy, and AB 2575 on clinical decision-support AI.

Newsom is the official responsible for the signings and vetoes, and in his message on SB 690 he said the bill addresses the "vexatious use of CIPA lawsuits and demand letters to extract settlement money from small businesses." The analysis comes from C. Jade Davis of the law firm Shumaker, Loop & Kendrick, who writes that California's market size and existing privacy infrastructure mean these laws will shape compliance programs well beyond the state. Davis expects plaintiffs to try to keep pending cases alive by adding wiretapping claims, while defendants may cite the California Supreme Court's decision in Californians for Disability Rights v. Mervyn's, which applied limits on private unfair competition suits to cases already pending. The firm advises businesses to review pending section 638.51 suits and demand letters, update deletion workflows, and inventory their AI and automated decision systems.

The changes arrive amid wider activity on privacy. Twenty states now have comprehensive privacy laws in effect, with Oklahoma, Alabama, Louisiana and Vermont enacting new ones in 2026, and amendments to the Connecticut Data Privacy Act took effect October 1, 2026. Under California's CCPA regulations, businesses must complete risk assessments for earlier covered activities by December 31, 2027, with an executive attestation and summary due April 1, 2028. First certifications for mandatory independent cybersecurity audits are phased in from April 1, 2028 through 2030, depending on business size.

stories.Headline: Harvard College students are using newly expanded access to Anthropic’s Claude for coursework, extracurricular projects, and personal tasks after the Faculty of Arts and Sciences began providing institutional access to the AI platform this summer. The FAS fir
stories.Summary:
Harvard College students are using newly widened access to Anthropic's Claude for coursework, extracurricular projects and personal tasks, according to the Harvard Crimson. The Faculty of Arts and Sciences began providing institutional access to the AI platform this summer. The change was first announced in April, when the FAS said it would add Claude to its suite of available AI tools while moving ChatGPT Edu to a request-only basis. The handover of tool availability to Harvard affiliates took place over the summer, and students are now in their first semester with the FAS-sponsored access.

Students described a wide range of uses. In General Education 1201, on neuroscience and artificial intelligence, Claude is built into the syllabus and assignments, which Iris A. Heikkinen '29 said teaches students how to use AI for studying. Leonardo Miranda '30 is using it in a first-year seminar called "Letting Claude Cook," where students must use the tool for a class project, and he said there is no cap on how many credits a student can use. Santiago D. Revilla '30 built a website that pulls in his Google Calendar and shows the weather for each day so he can plan walks and runs, while Ankit Biswas '30, a research fellow at the Cambridge Boston Align Initiative, uses Claude to scaffold ideas and handle implementation. Sean "Brady" Merrill '30 said he has used Claude Premium to help build models for a racing boat club he belongs to.

Responsibility for the rollout rests with the FAS, which made the April announcement and oversaw the summer transition. The seminar Miranda described is taught by Douglas P. Finkbeiner, the FAS's senior adviser on generative AI, who previously worked for Anthropic. Some students tied their preference for Claude to their views of the company. Merrill said he favors it because Anthropic's leadership and staff did not sign a deal with the Pentagon, a reference to a dispute earlier this year between Anthropic and the Department of Defense over AI safety safeguards. Conner M. Lewandowski '30 said he would rather support a company whose vision for AI and moral outlook match his own.

The Harvard access sits alongside a broader push by Anthropic into academia, including a new Guest Investigators program reported by Tech Times. The company opened a call on Wednesday for principal investigators at academic institutions, nonprofits and government labs to apply for embedded research collaborations lasting 8 to 12 weeks, with extensions possible for some projects. The program covers five life sciences areas, including causal human biology, drug discovery and clinical science, and excludes private companies and startups. Anthropic pays all model-compute costs, and researchers keep their data and the right to pursue follow-on work, while Anthropic commits to open-sourcing accompanying code and data and to publishing results jointly. The application window runs about 14 days from October 22, 2026, and Anthropic has said it will try to notify selected participants roughly 14 days after applications close.

stories.Headline: NCERT Introduces AI And Computational Thinking Module For Classes 9 To 12, Details Here
stories.Summary:
The National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) has introduced an introductory module on Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence for students in Classes 9 to 12. The council announced it on October 23, 2026, and the module is aligned with the vision of the National Education Policy 2020. It is built for beginners, so students do not need any earlier knowledge of artificial intelligence. Its stated aim is to help students understand AI, build problem-solving skills and learn to use emerging technologies responsibly.

The module presents Computational Thinking as a systematic way of identifying and solving problems, and it explains how AI works, where it can be applied and what its limits are. It follows an experiential, activity-based approach made up of discussions, practical exercises, experiments and reflection. All activities can be carried out with or without digital devices, which lets schools with different levels of digital infrastructure take part. A section on Aadhaar and UPI is included as examples of AI in India. The material also gives special weight to ethical and safe use, covering data privacy, misinformation, fairness and digital safety, and it teaches students to check AI-generated information rather than accept it at face value, while stressing human judgement and creativity.

NCERT issued the statement describing the module, and its director, Dinesh Prasad Saklani, wrote in the foreword that responsible and safe use of technology runs through the whole module. According to him, students are taught to protect personal information, verify what AI produces, recognise misleading content and seek help. NCERT said the module encourages critical thinking, creativity and problem-solving through hands-on learning. It added that the goal is to prepare learners to handle an AI-driven future with confidence, creativity and responsibility.

The module forms part of wider government efforts to bring Computational Thinking and AI into school education. In a Press Information Bureau statement dated August 5, 2026, the Ministry of Education said NCERT, working with the Central Board of Secondary Education, had introduced a dedicated curriculum on these subjects for Classes 3 to 8 from the 2026-27 academic year. The ministry also confirmed that the curriculum for Grades 9 to 12 in AI and allied subjects had been finalised. That framework centres on logical reasoning, pattern recognition, algorithm design and data literacy, along with the ethical and responsible use of AI. The articles do not say when the new module will be put to use in classrooms.

stories.Headline: Microsoft’s AI diagnostic tool outperforms general physicians in complex cases, study finds
stories.Summary:
Microsoft researchers have reported that an AI system they built diagnosed complex medical cases more accurately than practicing generalist physicians, according to a study published October 22, 2026 in Science. The system, called the Diagnostic Orchestrator, or DxO, runs on a commercial large language model, GPT-5 in the main results, and simulates a panel of physicians who track a differential diagnosis, challenge leading hypotheses and weigh the cost of each test. On 304 New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases it reached the correct diagnosis 83.2% of the time, versus 36.1% for generalist physicians who could use search and reference tools. On 325 emergency department admissions drawn from the MIMIC-IV-ED database, it scored 80.3%, against 46.8% for physicians.

The study built a benchmark called SDBench, in which each case begins with a brief clinical vignette and the diagnostician must decide what history to take, which tests to order and when to commit to a diagnosis. A separate AI gatekeeper released information only when asked, and test costs were estimated from hospital chargemaster pricing. Physicians averaged 22.3% accuracy without reference tools, and the best individual physician reached 51.8% on the conference cases and 62.5% on the emergency cases. Physicians asked 5.6 questions on average before ordering a first test, while DxO asked 25.5. Without budget limits, DxO's testing cost more than the physicians' ($5,431 versus $4,725 on the conference cases, $4,979 versus $3,400 on the emergency cases), but budget-limited versions scored 80.9% at $2,241 and 79.6% at $1,303 on the conference cases, and 73.2% at $2,634 and 69.5% at $2,037 on the emergency cases.

All 15 authors are Microsoft employees, including Microsoft AI chief executive Mustafa Suleyman, Dominic King and Eric Horvitz, and they hold equity in the company, which sells AI and health care services. Eight authors are named inventors on a Microsoft patent application tied to the evaluation framework, and the study had no outside funding. The authors argue that static benchmarks, which hand over a full case write-up at once, can overstate AI ability because they cannot show whether a system asks the right questions, avoids needless testing or knows when to stop. They suggested the AI's edge may come from its breadth of knowledge and its consistency, without fatigue, time pressure or cognitive bias.

The authors acknowledged limits. The comparison was against individual generalists, not specialists or teams, and they expect the gap to narrow against specialists matched to each case. The NEJM cases are chosen for teaching value, the benchmark was text-only with no imaging or pathology slides, and every case had a pathological diagnosis, so healthy and benign visits were left out. Cost estimates used standardized U.S. pricing, and the study did not assess treatment, patient safety or outcomes. Next, the authors plan to design workflows in which clinicians and AI work together, and see potential uses in medical education and continuing professional development.

stories.Headline: Why CoreWeave is at the center of the AI selloff
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, the AI cloud company, has become the focus of a broad selloff in artificial intelligence and technology stocks. CNBC reports that the company faces a crisis of confidence among both equity and bond investors, as interest rates spike and worries about the AI build-out grow. Many market participants now see debt-heavy "neocloud" firms like CoreWeave as the most vulnerable trade in the AI space. Reuters, via CNA, said CoreWeave's shares lost a quarter of their value in the week before October 19, as the company's $50 billion in debt set off the rout.

The damage spread well beyond one stock. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell more than 11 per cent that week and shed around $2 trillion in market value over an eight-session losing streak through Friday. Neocloud rival Nebius Group had tumbled more than 31 per cent over the previous two weeks, and Micron slid nearly 15 per cent. On Monday, October 19, AI stocks bounced back as government bond yields and crude oil prices eased. CoreWeave rose 2.4 per cent in choppy trading, Nebius gained 3.4 per cent, Applied Digital 8.5 per cent and IREN 5 per cent, while the yield on CoreWeave's 2031 bond fell 19.5 basis points to 15.13 per cent, down from more than 16 per cent the week before.

The trigger for the stumble, according to the Reuters report, was a hot inflation reading that raised bets on interest-rate hikes and fed fears that heavily indebted AI companies would face higher borrowing costs. Goldman Sachs responded by upgrading CoreWeave to "buy" from "neutral," arguing that tight computing capacity and the company's performance edge over other neoclouds should lift annual recurring revenue per megawatt over the next two years, and calling the pullback a buying opportunity. J.P. Morgan upgraded Intel to "neutral" from "underweight," citing rising agentic AI workloads and tight supplies of advanced chips. Intel rose 4.5 per cent, Nvidia 1.5 per cent, AMD 3.6 per cent and Broadcom 2.4 per cent.

Analysts were cautious about reading too much into the rebound. Thomas Hayes of Great Hill Capital called the debt issue a constant push-pull that will remain a factor, and said the move could be a dead cat bounce, since the bond market remains skeptical about financing the build-out without demanding ever higher yields. Looking ahead, Morgan Stanley expects total AI investment to reach $1.6 trillion in 2027 and $1.8 trillion in 2028. Earnings from big technology companies are seen as the next test, with Meta Platforms, Tesla and SpaceX reporting later that week, along with chip firms Lam Research, Texas Instruments and Western Digital. Jay Woods of Freedom Capital Markets said the question is whether investors are still willing to pay a premium for AI growth, not whether that growth will continue.

stories.Headline: MS GOP asks Attorney General to investigate Colom campaign AI video - The Clarion-Ledger
stories.Summary:
On October 22, 2026, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst asked Attorney General Lynn Fitch to investigate an AI-generated video posted by Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom that depicts his opponent, Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, fleeing questions and photographs from reporters. The video, posted about a month before the November 3 election on Facebook and Instagram, carries the caption "Based on a true story," and the party says the content was not real. Hurst's request came in a letter to Fitch's office, and the Clarion-Ledger reported it that day. The following day, on Friday, October 23, Fitch notified Colom and his campaign to remove the ads from their social media platforms, according to WLBT.

The state law at issue was passed in 2024 and bars sharing realistic altered photos or videos, known as digitizations, within 90 days of an election with the intent to injure a candidate. Under WLBT's account, violations tied to an intent to deter voting can carry up to five years in prison and fines of up to $10,000. The Clarion-Ledger reported that the statute itself sets a penalty of up to a year in prison, a $5,000 fine or both, and it also contains exceptions for satire and parody without defining either term. Fitch's office told Colom to take down the video by 5 p.m. that Friday or face a possible injunction, and WLBT reported that as of late morning the video remained online.

Hurst argued in his letter and a news release that the video is deception rather than satire or parody, because Colom labeled it as a true story and did not disclose that it was artificial. He also pointed to an earlier simulated phone call Colom posted when he launched his campaign in 2025, which the party said it referred to the FBI, the Department of Justice and the U.S. Attorney, though the Clarion-Ledger reported it was unclear whether any penalties followed. Colom's campaign manager, Gerard Henderson, called the request an act of desperation and an attempt to weaponize public office, and said Republicans are worried about November 3. WLBT reported that Democratic analyst Brandon Jones called the legal filing political nonsense. The Clarion-Ledger also notes the race has grown increasingly bitter, with nicknames, dueling fake campaign websites and Hyde-Smith's earlier resurfacing of an arrest report about Colom, and that Colom campaigns with Kamala Harris on October 22 while Donald Trump is scheduled to rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth on October 26.

stories.Headline: How governments around the world are shaping what AI can say about politics
stories.Summary:
A researcher at a nonpartisan think tank at Vanderbilt University, Jordi Calvet-Bademunt, wrote in The Conversation on October 20, 2026, that governments around the world are increasingly shaping what AI chatbots can say about politics. He cited a recent survey finding that about one in five American voters has asked chatbots about elections and politics, as the U.S. midterms approach. He and his colleagues worked with legal experts to study how governments in 12 countries and regions regulate AI, publishing reports in 2025 and 2026. Their finding was that governments often rely on existing rules, such as national security or anti-state propaganda laws, instead of writing new AI laws. Because many tech companies apply the same policies everywhere, the answers American voters receive may be shaped by governments at home and abroad.

The article lists several examples. In 2024, an Indian journalist asked Google's Gemini whether Prime Minister Narendra Modi's policies were fascist, and the government then required official permission before "unreliable" AI models could be released, though that requirement was later dropped. China requires AI models to uphold "socialist core values," and a Turkish court blocked Grok posts that allegedly insulted President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and religious values. In December 2025, a Vietnamese court sentenced two activists living in Germany to 17 years each in prison for spreading anti-state material, with prosecutors accusing them of using AI to fake the voices and images of Vietnamese leaders. The European Union's AI Act, adopted in 2024, requires any company offering AI tools in Europe to mark AI-generated content, and Anthropic applies the marks globally because it cannot reliably do so by region.

European regulators have also acted on political content more directly. In August 2026, the EU placed ChatGPT under the strictest tier of its Digital Services Act, so OpenAI must now assess and reduce systemic risks, including threats to elections such as disinformation. The Dutch Data Protection Authority tested four chatbots before the 2025 national election and found the political middle ground "virtually disappears" in their voting advice, urging providers to stop their systems being used for it. In 2024, Thierry Breton, then the EU's top digital rules enforcer, reminded Elon Musk of his legal obligations before Musk's live interview with Donald Trump on X. In the United States, a 2025 executive order on "Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government" requires AI models the government buys to be "truth-seeking" and ideologically neutral.

The author argues that "truth-seeking" can mean very different things to different people, noting that the president recently banned three news outlets from the White House and dismissed media polls as "fake." The Federal Trade Commission has suggested that AI companies steering answers toward undisclosed ideological objectives might break consumer protection law. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that eight in 10 Americans believe Republican and Democratic voters cannot agree on basic facts. Dozens of states have passed laws restricting AI-generated political deepfakes, and U.S. courts blocked the California and Hawaii laws, citing the First Amendment. The author advises voters to treat chatbot answers about elections as a starting point and not a substitute for their own critical thinking.

stories.Headline: India's Tech Mahindra partners with SpaceXSI for AI-powered software development - CNA
stories.Summary:
Tech Mahindra, the Indian IT services company, announced on Thursday, October 22, that it has partnered with SpaceXSI to use artificial intelligence to modernise legacy applications and speed up software development. Reuters-style coverage described Tech Mahindra as India's fifth-largest IT firm. The company will also bring in the chatbot Grok Build to set up industry-specific solutions. The announcement did not say when the joint offering will become available.

The deal combines Tech Mahindra's engineering and enterprise transformation services with SpaceXSI's development platform. The two sides plan to concentrate on software delivery, code quality and developer productivity across technology, telecommunications, banking and financial services, manufacturing, healthcare and retail. They also intend to run joint go-to-market initiatives, customer engagements and industry-specific programmes. Tech Mahindra will set up enablement and certification programmes to help client engineering teams adopt the tools.

Toni Adams, Head of Global Partnerships at SpaceXSI, said in the announcement that most enterprises already accept that AI will change how software is built. What they lack, she said, is expertise in rolling it out across large and varied engineering teams without breaking what already works. Tech Mahindra said it will fold Grok Build expertise into its engineering transformation and application modernisation services. The companies described the offering as designed for enterprise settings, where governance, security and compliance are requirements.

Tech Mahindra already has similar pacts with Google Gemini and Microsoft, but this is the first time an Indian IT major has teamed up with the AI division of rocket maker SpaceX. The company did not name any customer deployments, disclose financial terms or put a figure on expected productivity gains. It has also not said how much revenue, if any, it expects the collaboration to bring in. Separately, Tech Mahindra plans to report its AI revenue on its own starting in the second half of fiscal 2027.

stories.Headline: Kansas City lab to train AI to predict protein changes tied to ALS, Alzheimer’s
stories.Summary:
A Kansas City research lab has been chosen to take part in a $28.6 million national effort to train artificial intelligence to predict protein changes linked to neurodegenerative disease. KCTV reported the news on October 21, 2026. Investigator Randal Halfmann and a team of local scientists at the Stowers Institute for Medical Research received a $4.1 million grant as their share of the project. They will use technology in new ways to help predict harmful protein changes tied to Alzheimer's, Huntington's and ALS.

Halfmann's lab will produce more than 10 billion measurements covering 50,000 proteins and over a million samples. This data is meant to teach AI to recognize the moment when something begins to go wrong. The task is hard because AI can readily detect many proteins but struggles with those involved in diseases such as Alzheimer's, which keep changing shape. The microscopic protein clumping under study will be collected at a level of detail never achieved before.

Halfmann said the question behind the work has motivated biology for roughly 60 years. He believes the effort will lay groundwork for generations, and his ultimate aim is to predict when a person will develop a disease and how quickly it will progress. He expects the data to create a much larger pool of people entering clinical trials, which would give those trials the power to find therapies that work. He also said he is optimistic that in two years researchers will be in a much better position to act.

His team has been working on this problem for years, and in 2023 the Stowers lab first identified the molecular trigger behind toxic protein buildup in Huntington's disease. With millions of Americans affected by neurodegenerative disease, Halfmann said the situation creates a sense of urgency, and he does not take any day for granted because every day matters to patients. The $28.6 million effort brings together select scientists from a handful of top institutions and universities around the country. KCTV pointed readers to the project's website for more on this and other research.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind Staff Resign Over Military AI Contracts
stories.Summary:
Several researchers at Google DeepMind have resigned, or are reportedly preparing to leave, over the company's growing military work, according to BBC interviews cited by Yahoo. Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer who joined DeepMind in 2023, quit this week and sent an internal letter urging colleagues to "stay human." She told the BBC and The Intercept that she lost faith in the company's stated ethics because of its work with the US and Israeli militaries. A second researcher, Andreas Kirsch, also resigned and said Google's governance and oversight were not strong enough for safe deployment in classified military settings. Kirsch reportedly added that Google may have little real power to monitor or veto how the Pentagon uses its technology once it sits inside classified systems.

The departures follow Reuters reporting that Google signed a classified agreement with the US Department of Defense allowing its AI models to be used for "any lawful government purpose," including classified military work. According to Reuters, the deal says the systems should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or for autonomous weapons without proper human oversight and control. The same agreement reportedly requires Google to help adjust its AI safety settings and filters when the government asks, which could allow some safeguards to be changed. Liguori said she began a personal sick-out the day after Google announced the Pentagon contract in April, using sick leave and holiday time. She had first grown uneasy after learning of Project Nimbus, the Google and Amazon cloud and AI contract worth $1.2 billion that supplies tools to Israel's government and military.

Google told the BBC that it applies a consistent contract-review process tied to its acceptable-use policies and AI principles, and that staff can raise concerns without fear of retaliation. The company says its published principles call for human oversight and for alignment with international law and human rights. Google also said at the time that Project Nimbus was not meant for sensitive military or intelligence work involving weapons or intelligence services. An Israeli government minister has rejected claims about AI-assisted targeting linked to that contract, calling them false and distorted in comments tied to a documentary, per the BBC.

Google is not alone in pursuing such work, as the BBC reports that OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia and Reflection have also signed or sought US military AI arrangements. Former Project Maven director Jack Shanahan, a retired lieutenant general, warned that pressure to deploy can outrun careful testing and evaluation. Sarah Shoker, a former head of geopolitics at OpenAI, told the BBC that AI shortens the time for decisions, making it hard for a human to check hundreds of AI-selected targets for mistakes. Pentagon officials have described speed as central to winning in AI-driven warfare, according to the BBC. The articles do not say whether more resignations will follow or whether Google will change the terms of the contract.

stories.Headline: Recursive Releases Flint, an Open-Weight 40B MoE Local Coding Model for Agents with 2.5B Active Params
stories.Summary:
Recursive Superintelligence has released Flint, its first model, and posted the weights on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license. Flint is a mixture-of-experts model built for local coding agents, with about 39.8 billion total parameters and roughly 2.5 billion active per token. It is text-only, supports reasoning and OpenAI-compatible tool calls, and is meant to investigate codebases, fix bugs, implement features and write tests. The company says its Eureka Machine, an automated research system, helped build nearly every part of the stack. A second article published two days later covers a separate release from Moonshot AI, Kimi K3.1 Pro, described as a mixture-of-experts model with 2.8 trillion total and 104 billion active parameters and a 1 million token context, but the text provided cuts off before giving details.

On hardware, Flint is meant to run on 48 GB Apple Silicon Macs, including M4 Pro, M5 Pro and M5 Max, or on 48 GB NVIDIA GPUs, and its 4-bit weights take about 23 GB. The model card documents a context of 262,144 tokens, though the company blog cites up to 512k. Its architecture has 49 layers, two dense and 47 mixture-of-experts, with 256 routed experts per layer, six chosen per token plus one always-active shared expert. Attention mixes two types: 35 layers use a 513-token sliding window and 14 use full attention with no positional encoding, with 32 query heads and 4 key/value heads. The 2.5 billion active figure includes the output head, and the active body alone is about 2.2 billion.

The Eureka Machine proposes ideas, implements and tests them, and picks what to try next. It began from a baseline with 35 billion total and 3 billion active parameters, then searched expert configurations and widths to reach the final size. It also quantized the output layer to 4 bits, against common practice, and an offline distillation stage using the 16-bit model as teacher recovered accuracy, nearly halving training steps versus a quantization-aware baseline. The resulting NVFP4 model scores within 0.7 points of the 16-bit version, and the system wrote specialized kernels, including a Metal megakernel that fuses the full decode pass on M4 and M5 chips. All benchmark scores are self-reported by Recursive, using temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 and top-k 20.

On those benchmarks, the 16-bit model scores 54.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 89.7% on SWE-bench Pro v2, 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified, 80.3% on LiveCodeBench v6, 89.2% on IFBench and 95.1% on IFEval, with the NVFP4 version close behind on each. Recursive's chart puts Flint at the top among mixture-of-experts models under 50 billion parameters for agentic coding, ahead of Qwen 3.6 at 73.4% on SWE-bench Verified, though it trails the strongest dense models. Its weakest result is Terminal-Bench 2.1, where dense Qwen 3.8 scores 73.0%. Terminal-Bench used the Terminus 2 harness and counted solutions found through web retrieval as failures, while SWE-bench runs used mini-swe-agent without internet access. Agentic scores average pass@1 over at least five attempts, and the company claims speeds above 125 tokens per second on a MacBook Pro and above 150 on an RTX Spark.

stories.Headline: Ukrainian drone strikes hit five Russian data centers, disrupting cloud services and AI work
stories.Summary:
Ukrainian drones struck five Russian data centers this month, the Associated Press reported on October 22, 2026, and experts expect the damage to take months, perhaps years, to repair. Three of the sites belong to Yandex, Russia's largest technology company, one to Sberbank, the country's biggest bank, and one serves VKontakte, its main social network. The first strike, on October 8, hit a Yandex data center in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, which houses two of the company's three supercomputers. Yandex sites in Kaluga and Vladimir followed on October 9 and October 11, then Sberbank's data center and AI hub in Balakovo, in the Saratov region, on October 14. Four days later a data center in Saint Petersburg serving VKontakte was hit.

Yandex, Sberbank and VKontakte have said little about the damage, but people and businesses across Russia reported lasting interruptions to cloud services. Banking, online shopping, maps and ride hailing were hit, along with Yandex's voice assistant Alisa and AI chatbots, and arbitration courts reportedly called off or delayed hearings after losing access to databases. One Moscow resident told the AP he could not collect an online order, and a taxi driver said he lost fares because the Yandex app would not connect him with passengers. Yandex said it restored most of its key cloud services within days by shifting work to its other Russian data centers. The company had rehearsed losing one of its six data centers, but not three in four days.

The heavier blow is to Russia's AI work. Yandex's three supercomputers, which it uses to build its models, rank among the world's 500 most powerful, and the one at Sasovo was ranked 19th. Satellite images pointed to serious damage, and observers said fires probably ruined high-end chips and other equipment. Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society, an activist group, told the AP the strikes leave Russia far behind in the AI race, and that sanctions and a global chip shortage could make repairs slow, costly or impossible. Connor Martin, an analyst cited by the AP, wrote that Russia will struggle to replace the American-designed chips inside the Yandex machines.

The attacks follow Russian strikes on data centers in Ukraine that disrupted internet and television services, part of a wider campaign by each side against the other's infrastructure. Ukraine has hit Russian oil refineries and the warehouses of the online retailers Wildberries and Ozon. Nick Reiners, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said Russia lacks the air defenses to cover so large a country, and that its rule keeping data inside its borders has made that data easier to knock out. Iranian drones earlier hit two Amazon Web Services data centers in the United Arab Emirates and one in Bahrain, and AWS said last month it could not restore access to resources and data at two of them. Klimarev expects many Russian companies to rent computing capacity in Europe as a result.

stories.Headline: Mistral Advances AI for Engineering with NVIDIA
stories.Summary:
Mistral and NVIDIA announced on October 21, 2026 that they are collaborating to create AI-native engineering workflows using NVIDIA accelerated computing. The work combines Mistral Large 4, Mistral’s data generation and physics modeling pipelines, and NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries and NVIDIA Warp. It also connects Mistral’s models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for GPU-accelerated 3D scene generation and SimReady asset creation. The companies will develop public benchmarks and open datasets for evaluating physics models, giving researchers and industrial teams a shared way to compare model accuracy and performance. They will also create evaluations for agentic AI in computer-aided engineering and electronic design automation for aerospace, automotive, and semiconductor use cases.

The collaboration builds on an existing partnership that produced Mistral NeMo and now includes work through the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition on a frontier base model. Mistral Large 4, known as Le Chonk, has about 1 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active parameters, and it was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral-operated data centers in Europe. Its weights are planned for release at the end of October. Mistral is also bringing additional NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure online as part of a compute roadmap targeting 1 GW of capacity by 2030. Neil Ashton, Mistral’s vice president of computational engineering, said the pace of engineering has been set by the pace of simulation, and the partnership gives engineers faster simulation cycles and open benchmarks rigorous enough to validate agents on real CAE and EDA work.

Tim Costa, NVIDIA’s vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering, said the next wave of engineering breakthroughs will come from exploring ideas that were once too complex or time-consuming to test. He said combining Mistral’s open models and physics AI expertise with NVIDIA accelerated computing helps engineers push design boundaries, with shared industry benchmarks to build confidence in AI. The companies say this work will help define standards for agentic and physics AI evaluations in engineering, establishing consistent and reproducible methods for assessing capabilities and tracking progress. The initiative aims to accelerate engineering simulation and enable closed-loop workflows that connect simulation, AI model development, and engineering design. Mistral and NVIDIA say the expansion strengthens Europe’s role in developing and delivering AI for the world by connecting European infrastructure and research with open models and specialized engineering capabilities.

stories.Headline: Microsoft says China-linked hackers used AI penetration testing tool ARTEX to compromise ConnectWise as part of a campaign targeting hundreds of organizations (AJ Vicens/Reuters)
stories.Summary:
Microsoft said on Wednesday that a China state-aligned actor it tracks as Storm-0940 was behind the recent supply chain compromise of the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application. According to Microsoft, the group used ARTEX, a Go-based agentic AI penetration testing framework, to speed up scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse against downstream victims. ARTEX was made closed-source after it was abused in attacks on South Korean financial institutions. Microsoft said the actor ran the tool at "machine speed" to target hundreds of organizations around the world since September 2026.

Microsoft listed a broad set of targeted sectors, including aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductors, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits. In the ConnectWise incident, ARTEX was seen trying to sign in to more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 attempts per minute, a pace Microsoft said leaves defenders only a short window to respond. Between October 10 and 14, 2026, infrastructure at 144.172.64[.]99 ran an automated cross-tenant password-spray campaign against 327 accounts at eight organizations, aiming at Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online. Microsoft captured more than 151,000 failed logon events in that window, peaking on October 11 at 2,900 failures per minute and more than 111,000 failures in a single day. Forty-eight accounts received over 1,000 failures each, though Microsoft detected no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call or directory change during that period.

That changed on October 15, 2026, when the AI agents gained access to the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications and began using them to authenticate into customer environments. Microsoft said this let the actor operate without an interactive user sign-in, because the applications had already been granted access. Follow-on activity included reconnaissance, changes to application credentials and attempts to alter privileges that could allow wider or lasting access. In a chunk of the ARTEX-driven attacks, the adversary gained privileged access to an organization's cloud infrastructure, and in several cases less than three hours passed between first targeting and privileged access.

Microsoft is the source of the findings, and The Hacker News reported on its disclosure, which Reuters also covered. The company first detailed Storm-0940 in November 2024, when it described a botnet called Quad7, also known as CovertNetwork-1658, used for highly evasive password spray attacks. Microsoft assesses the group has been active since at least 2021. It is also known to exploit internet-facing applications for initial access, move through environments using compromised accounts, and keep access by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications in cloud infrastructure so it can reach Microsoft 365 resources. The articles do not say what steps ConnectWise or affected customers will take next.

stories.Headline: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang joined on stage by robot ducks as he hails Europe’s AI potential
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang delivered the keynote at the company's GTC conference in Berlin on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at the tent-shaped Tempodrom. The presentation was briefly interrupted by environmental protesters who held up banners and demanded that the company clean up its act, before security removed them. Huang joked that the issues were important but asked to finish his talk first. He also brought small two-legged Microduck robots from Pollen Robotics onto the stage, where they responded to his voice commands by lying down and rolling over, and beeped back at him.

The main hardware announcement was DSX POD, a reference design for factory-built, containerized AI infrastructure that combines seven liquid-cooled Vera Rubin compute racks using Nvidia's Spectrum-X networking. Partners will cable, integrate and test the systems in modular containers before delivery, with availability expected in early 2027. Nvidia says deployment could shrink from six months to as little as 14 days at a prepared site, though that leaves out the work of getting power and connectivity ready first. Huang said the systems use closed-loop liquid cooling with coolant temperatures up to 45°C, and claimed that at 2 gigawatts the design could save 54 million litres of water a day. He also unveiled Agile ONE SN, a humanoid robot reference platform from German startup Agile Robots, built on Nvidia's Isaac GR00T technology and a Jetson Thor compute module and scheduled for early 2027.

Huang called robotics the next great industry and said that everyone will become an AI company. He added that Nvidia's Hyperion car system is being adopted by more vendors and that European telecoms operators are deploying Nvidia-powered computing for AI-RAN. Forrester principal analyst Paul Miller said Huang cast Nvidia as a strong supporter of Europe's sovereign tech ambitions, noting that the company has invested almost $10 billion in Europe over the past year, including 14 investments in European startups during this trip. Miller cautioned that Nvidia is not a European firm, so anything critically dependent on it is unlikely to meet the purest definitions of European tech sovereignty. Speaking to CNBC, Huang said the demand for capital is much greater than its availability, though he added that this will get solved.

The Berlin event capped a week-and-a-half tour of Europe in which Huang met leaders including U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. CNBC reported that the conference ended amid a selloff in neocloud stocks, with CoreWeave down 10% and Nebius down 7% at the close, on concerns about heavy borrowing. Huang put the cost of a 1 gigawatt data center at about $50 billion, while Goldman Sachs estimates AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031. One infrastructure financing executive told CNBC that capital will soon become the bottleneck. Huang's trip was not over, as he was due in Kazakhstan next to promote its potential as an AI hub.

stories.Headline: Micron Technology Maps AI Memory Future With HBM, DRAM and NAND Roadmap
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology laid out a technology and product roadmap during a leadership webinar, built around the growing memory and storage demands of artificial intelligence. Scott DeBoer, the company's president and chief technology and products officer, said AI is turning memory from a supporting part into a central limit on system performance, capacity and cost per token. He said Micron intends to advance memory, storage and compute together, with higher bandwidth, larger capacities, better power efficiency and closer work with customers. The company said it is already in high-volume manufacturing with its 1-gamma DRAM node and with HBM4, and is developing both standard and customized high-bandwidth memory.

On the schedule, Micron expects its 1-delta DRAM node to reach volume production in the second half of 2027, aiming for a mid-20% improvement in bit density and tuning it for AI products such as HBM5, vertical HBM and vertical edge inference memory. Its Generation 11 NAND is also due to ramp in the second half of 2027, with more than 400 layers, wafer-on-wafer bonding, more than double the bit density of Generation 9, and a target of 1.5 times the I/O speed. LPDDR6 is expected to deliver 35% better power performance than LPDDR5, and Micron is working with customers on DDR6, which it said would offer twice the bandwidth of DDR5. The company also plans a 1-terabyte RDIMM, following its recently sampled 512-gigabyte DDR5 RDIMM. Future HBM base dies will use foundry nodes, and while HBM4 did not need more advanced CMOS, HBM4E will.

DeBoer was the main voice on the technical choices. He said Micron is confident in several more generations of planar DRAM scaling before it brings in 3D DRAM, and that the timing of 3D will turn on cost, complexity and device performance. He rejected the idea that 4F² designs inherently beat 6F² designs on density, saying capacitor pitch is what fundamentally sets DRAM bit density, and that fundamental problems with 4F² scaling will eventually lead 3D DRAM to take its place. He described vertical HBM, which puts memory directly on top of processing units, as aimed mainly at much greater bandwidth, with capacity scaling more slowly because of heat. He said hybrid bonding is needed as interconnect pitches tighten, and that the company is developing higher-stack HBM and thermal measures such as heat spreaders over the hotter parts of an HBM base die.

For context, Micron said it uses AI internally to speed up its own work, citing a data center controller design that went from silicon to tape-out in half the time of the prior generation and an SSD effort finished with 60% less time. It pointed to longer-term investments including Micron Ventures, work at Albany NanoTech on advanced lithography and a previously announced $10 billion, 10-year commitment to Micron Research Labs. DeBoer said the company is collaborating with partners from startup Liqid to Meta, and that Micron and Meta recently published a white paper on optimizing LPDDR6 for data centers. He added that Micron does not expect memory supply to come into balance over the next two years, citing earlier comments by company leadership.

stories.Headline: LG Electronics to Bring Robots, AI to World's Largest Tidal Power Plant
stories.Summary:
LG Electronics signed a memorandum of understanding with Korea Water Resources Corporation, known as K-water, on Oct. 22 at the Sihwa Tidal Culture Center in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province. The agreement covers the Sihwa Lake tidal power plant, which has the largest generation capacity of any tidal plant in the world. The two sides agreed to turn the facility into an AI-powered smart plant, applying digital twins and robots on site. They also agreed to cooperate on research and development, policy and expansion abroad.

The company will first use digital twin technology to copy the whole plant in a virtual space and link it to real-time data from generation equipment and closed-circuit cameras. That setup is meant to allow forecasts of power output, testing of operating scenarios and diagnosis of equipment conditions. LG is also considering an AI agent built on Exaone, the proprietary model from LG AI Research, to analyze output losses, spot equipment faults, support predictive maintenance, assess risks and tune inspection schedules. For work on site, patrol robots, AI-equipped cameras and industrial robots would handle facility patrols, equipment inspections, monitoring of hazardous areas, and the storage and transport of spare parts.

Lee Seung-ki, head of LG Electronics' Smart Factory Solution Center, said it is significant that skills built on manufacturing floors are now being applied to public infrastructure. He said the company will work with K-water to support the plant's digital transformation and keep improving its operating efficiency and safety. The Korea Times reported the company's statement in similar terms. LG framed the project as a reference case for taking its smart factory solutions into energy infrastructure at home and overseas.

The deal marks the first time LG has carried smart factory technology from manufacturing into public infrastructure such as power plants, according to The Elec. The company wants to grow beyond its existing manufacturing and logistics clients and join energy projects led by governments and large corporations. Cumulative orders for its smart factory solutions business passed 1 trillion won in the first half of 2026, two years after the unit's launch. The articles describe the digital twin, AI agent and robotics work as items to be examined or tested, and they give no timeline or cost for the upgrades.

stories.Headline: LTM Launches BlueVerse Industrial AI Lab in Chennai
stories.Summary:
LTM, an IT services and consulting company, has launched its BlueVerse Industrial AI Lab in Chennai, according to an article published on October 23, 2026. The lab is meant to help enterprises develop, simulate and validate AI solutions for industrial operations and intelligent products before they are deployed. LTM said clients, technology partners and its own teams can use the facility. It is designed for industrial sites that have legacy equipment, limited connectivity and hazardous working conditions.

The lab will combine LTM's industrial AI solutions, intellectual property and patents with small language models built for manufacturing. Its capabilities will include multispectral computer vision, edge devices, digital twins and industrial AI agents to support operational decision-making. A dedicated robotics zone will support work on autonomous mobile robots, collaborative robots and drones for inspection and material handling. The lab will also support engineering and testing for consumer electronics and medical technology devices, covering embedded software, on-device AI, interoperability, reliability, performance and applicable safety and regulatory requirements.

Gururaj Deshpande, Chief Delivery Officer at LTM, said industrial businesses are looking to shorten time to market, increase operational availability, improve worker safety and strengthen regulatory compliance. In his view, industrial AI offers powerful levers for reaching those goals. LTM also said its industrial AI teams, domain practitioners, technology partners and start-up ecosystem have together scaled more than 100 industrial AI solutions worldwide. The article noted that moving industrial AI from pilots to production remains difficult because systems must adapt to each facility, and that on-site deployment is a key hurdle.

The launch follows other efforts by Indian IT services companies to bring AI into manufacturing. In September, Tech Mahindra partnered with industrial technology company Infinite Uptime to bring physical AI into manufacturing workflows. Separately, LTM, a Larsen & Toubro Group company, launched BlueVerse ValueMesh, an AI execution platform for Oracle transformation programmes, and is presenting it at Oracle AI World 2026 in Las Vegas at booth 5020. The company has more than 87,000 employees across 40 countries. The articles do not say when the Chennai lab will begin operating or what comes next for it.

stories.Headline: OpenAI to bring AI models to Google's cloud, in further expansion beyond Microsoft
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on October 21, 2026 that its artificial intelligence models will become available to developers through Google’s cloud, after years of competition between the two companies. The ChatGPT maker will place its GPT products in Google Cloud’s model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks. This follows the end of Microsoft’s exclusive license on OpenAI’s intellectual property less than six months earlier. The day after that exclusivity ended, Amazon announced plans to host OpenAI models, and now Google is doing the same. The move puts OpenAI’s models on all three of the top U.S. cloud infrastructure providers.

The expansion reflects OpenAI’s push to reach enterprise developers and build its business beyond its consumer roots. Google Cloud’s annualized revenue growth accelerated to about 82 percent in the second quarter from 63 percent in the first quarter, partly due to demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second quarter cloud growth of 37 percent and 42 percent respectively. OpenAI is courting investors at a 1.4 trillion dollar valuation and targeting an initial public offering. Google and OpenAI previously partnered last year, when OpenAI used Google’s cloud to run ChatGPT and its application programming interface.

OpenAI said in a blog post that Google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them. Google introduced a new Gemini agent on October 8, 2026, designed to handle work across email, documents, spreadsheets and other business tools, planning tasks and connecting to company systems from a single interface. The company said its latest enterprise agent offering combines access to company information and business applications with administrative controls and governance features. OpenAI is also developing workplace agents that can take on tasks across business applications.

The broader context is that enterprise AI is shifting from a race for intelligence, speed, benchmarks and reasoning toward turning that intelligence into work businesses can consistently trust. Businesses cannot delegate accountability to a model, and organizations must decide which work AI should support, which it should complete and where human judgment must remain. The next enterprise AI race will not be won simply by having the smartest model, but by companies that know what they want that intelligence to do and build systems that allow them to trust the result. Separately, Microsoft and Google are backing three retired U.S. nuclear reactor restarts in Michigan, Pennsylvania and Iowa that could together deliver 2.25 gigawatts, with restarts targeted between 2027 and 2029.

stories.Headline: Europe RAISEs the Stakes for AI in Science
stories.Summary:
Businesses that use artificial intelligence face growing legal risk when what they tell people about their data practices does not match how their systems work, according to an analysis by Gouchev Law reported by PYMNTS on October 21, 2026. The analysis found a shared expectation among the Federal Trade Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission and European authorities that companies explain their AI practices accurately to users. It says that means tying disclosures to real data flows, vendor arrangements and model development, and dealing with changes before they take effect. The article does not say Europe is raising stakes for AI in science, so the story it actually covers is about corporate disclosure and regulatory scrutiny.

The analysis says the FTC is concerned about firms that collect information under one set of promises and later widen its use without enough transparency. A company that promised not to share customer data without consent, for example, could be exposed if it later sends chat transcripts to an outside AI provider for optimization. It cited FTC guidance warning that adopting more permissive practices through a "surreptitious, retroactive amendment" to contract terms or privacy policies may be unfair or deceptive. The analysis cautioned that a routine terms-update email, a website footer link or continued use of a product may not count as adequate acceptance of a material change. It also said broad statements that data helps improve services may fall short if they do not explain consequential AI uses, especially when customer inputs could train generative AI models.

The SEC adds another dimension, the analysis said, because AI disclosures must accurately reflect how systems are developed, trained and deployed. Marketing that overstates capabilities or mischaracterizes real use can create disclosure risk, and the FTC likewise looks at misleading product claims and omissions of material limitations. European data protection and consumer authorities, it added, are applying transparency, accountability and purpose-limitation principles to AI, while AI-specific frameworks bring expectations on risk classification, governance and controls across a system's lifecycle. Liability can also arise through customer contracts, as in an unnamed company's case, where a third-party AI vendor kept and reused customer content for model improvement and confidential material surfaced in other customers' workspaces. That dispute involved breach-of-contract allegations and ended in a six-figure settlement.

To lower exposure, the analysis recommended a joint assessment by legal, product and engineering teams. Businesses should list their deployed and upcoming AI systems, identify what information each one accesses, and map the outside vendors and APIs involved in processing. The results should guide updates to customer agreements, privacy policies and terms of use, which should say what is collected, processed and stored, how models interact with it, which providers take part and whether users can opt out. Vendor agreements should cover retention, model training and reuse in a way that matches customer commitments, and policies should be reviewed as products change, with legal and compliance involved before launch. The aim, the analysis said, is to make disclosures an accurate account of current operations and planned changes, closing the gaps that invite enforcement and contract claims.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Stocks To Research – October 22nd
stories.Summary:
On October 22nd, 2026, MarketBeat's stock screener tool flagged five artificial intelligence stocks to watch: Hut 8, Tempus AI, SentinelOne, Appian and Upstart. The list was published that day by the Markets Daily site, under the byline of Michael Walen. The companies were picked because they had the highest dollar trading volume of any AI stocks over the last several days. A similar list appeared on October 20th on the Ticker Report site, written by Ethan Ryder, and it carried three of the same names plus two others.

The October 22nd list describes each company briefly. Hut 8 builds and runs data centers for digital asset mining, computing and AI in the United States, and it reports in four segments: Digital Assets Mining, Managed Services, High Performance Computing Colocation and Cloud, and Other. Tempus AI applies artificial intelligence to precision medicine, giving physicians tools for personalized care while also supporting the discovery and delivery of therapeutics. SentinelOne is a cybersecurity provider whose Singularity Platform uses AI to prevent, detect and respond to threats across endpoints, cloud workloads and identity credentials. Appian offers a low-code platform covering AI, process automation, data fabric and process mining, while Upstart runs a cloud-based AI lending platform for personal loans, auto loans, home equity lines of credit and small dollar loans, connecting borrowers with banks and credit unions.

The earlier list, covering October 19th, kept Hut 8, Tempus AI and SentinelOne, and swapped in Ambarella and Exyn Technologies for Appian and Upstart. Ambarella designs semiconductors for high-definition and ultra HD video compression, image processing and AI vision. Exyn Technologies describes itself as a pioneer in autonomous robotics and AI for complex environments where GPS is unavailable. Both articles were produced by MarketBeat's screener, which means the selections come from a trading-volume ranking rather than from an editorial judgment about the companies' prospects.

The articles define AI stocks as shares of public companies that develop, provide or heavily use technologies such as machine learning, data analytics, robotics and AI-enabled software and hardware. They note that such stocks can give investors exposure to the growth of the AI industry, but that performance can be affected by competition, regulation, high valuations and the fast pace of technological change. The pieces say nothing about what any of the five companies will do next, and they report no price moves or analyst ratings. Both pages also point readers to related MarketBeat coverage, including a list of top stocks to own in October 2026.

stories.Headline: Attorney General Ken Paxton Sues OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman for Lying to Users and Harming Texans
stories.Summary:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a lawsuit on Friday, October 23, 2026, against OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman. The suit accuses the company of harming consumers through its ChatGPT chatbot despite marketing it as safe and reliable. Paxton says the company has failed to protect Texans, including children, from the dangers of relying on the tool. The complaint was announced in a press release from his office.

The lawsuit rests on two Texas laws, the Deceptive Trade Practices—Consumer Protection Act and the Securing Children Online through Parental Empowerment (SCOPE) Act. The first claim argues that OpenAI misled the public about ChatGPT's safety, accuracy, and reliability. The SCOPE Act, passed in 2023 during the 88th Legislative Session, is meant to stop digital services from signing up minors without parental or guardian consent. The second claim says ChatGPT did not require the age verification that law calls for. The suit also seeks to hold Altman personally liable for the alleged violations and for statements he has made about the company's products.

Paxton holds OpenAI responsible for what he describes as a series of serious harms. In the lawsuit, he says mass shooters have been aided in deadly attacks, vulnerable people have been encouraged toward suicide, and minors have become addicted to a tool that collects their data without parental oversight. He ties these harms to the company's drive to win the AI race and build large fortunes. In his own words, Paxton said OpenAI has a responsibility to protect users and warn them of the platform's dangers, and that he will fight to keep powerful technology companies from acting above the law.

The case arrives as AI has become a major political issue in Texas. Paxton has made opposition to AI data centers a central theme of his U.S. Senate campaign, and both he and his Democratic opponent, state Rep. James Talarico, accuse each other of being pro-AI. The Texan reports that OpenAI had not yet responded to the allegations at the time of publication. The articles do not say how the court will rule or how long the case may take.

stories.Headline: Florida Attorney General Proposes New Law Restricting Social Media, App Downloads and AI Chatbots for Minors
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has proposed a sweeping new law aimed at restricting social media, app downloads and AI chatbots for minors. The proposal, called the Safe Screens Act, would require parental consent before minors download or purchase apps. It follows an October 14 ruling by the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that allowed Florida to enforce its existing restrictions on social media accounts for children under 14. The legislation remains a proposal and would need approval from Florida lawmakers before it could become law. The bill would require social media companies to set stricter defaults for users ages 14 to 17.

Teenagers would be limited to two hours of social media use per day and 60 hours per month, and access would be blocked from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. daily and from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. on school weekdays.

Autoplay and infinite scrolling would be turned off by default unless a verified parent authorizes them, and public likes and reaction counts would be hidden unless a parent enables them. AI chatbot operators would be barred from offering romantic or emotional companionship features to children, and from encouraging suicide, self-harm, eating disorders or illegal activity. App stores and device operating systems would also have to verify ages, link minors to a parent or guardian, and require parental approval for downloads and purchases. Uthmeier said parents deserve real control and that companies must design for safety rather than addiction.

He argued that if platforms invite Florida's children onto their services, they have a duty to keep them safe. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd praised the proposal and said stronger enforcement is needed to keep large social media and gaming companies from exploiting children. Under the bill, the Attorney General's Office would gain enforcement authority, with penalties of up to $50,000 per violation for companies that knowingly or recklessly break the rules. The proposal would also require human review of child sexual exploitation reports within 48 hours and a one-strike policy for adult offenders.

stories.Headline: New AI-powered mosquito trap could help curb dengue outbreaks - University of South Florida
stories.Summary:
Florida is facing one of its worst dengue outbreaks in nearly a century, and a smart mosquito trap built by University of South Florida startup Digitomy is being tested as a way to slow it. The trap uses patented artificial intelligence and has reached more than 98 percent accuracy in identifying mosquito species during laboratory testing. Its research has been running at USF since 2018 and is supported by the National Science Foundation. Associate Professor Ryan Carney and Professor Sriram Chellappan developed the technology. The system is designed to help officials track disease-carrying mosquitoes more quickly.

The trap hangs from a low branch or sits on the ground, using a light or bait to draw mosquitoes in with a fan. Once insects land on a sticky pad, two built-in cameras photograph them so the AI can match them against a large database of mosquito images. Chellappan said traditional surveillance by specialists can take two to three days under a microscope, while the AI speeds up that process and still keeps people in charge. The team's partnership with the Anastasia Mosquito Control District in St. Johns County has helped advance the technology. The district's executive director, Rui-De Xue, said the work will help the district explore new AI tools and monitor mosquito populations more closely.

Beyond identifying species, the system could help health officials find where disease-carrying mosquitoes are concentrated and direct control efforts more precisely. It could also work alongside Carney's earlier DYCAST early warning system for dengue and West Nile virus outbreaks. The team has added trap data to its Global Mosquito Observations Dashboard, which already draws on more than half a million citizen science reports. Digitomy is also building a cloud-based education platform that lets control professionals and the public practice species identification and receive AI feedback without in-person training. Carney stressed that public habits matter too, urging people to drain standing water, cover their skin and use DEET.

The researchers are preparing for field validation with Hillsborough County as Digitomy moves toward consumer sales. Carney and Chellappan are working with USF Technology Transfer to license the technology to established trap manufacturers so they can add USF's identification system to existing equipment. Diana Shapiro, Digitomy's chief operations officer, said the goal is to give control programs same-day results rather than multi-day waits. This summer, Digitomy received a $25,000 award from USF's commercialization program to help speed licensing. The researchers hope to bring the platform into professional training and public education programs with mosquito control districts, including Anastasia and Hillsborough.

stories.Headline: As AI transforms education, a UF mathematician aims to preserve the productive struggle of learning
stories.Summary:
A University of Florida-led research team has built an AI tool called HaLLMos that gives students feedback on their mathematical proofs without handing them complete solutions. The project was announced in an October 23, 2026 news release from the university. Its aim is to keep students engaged in difficult but achievable problems, a process educators call productive struggle. The team argues that the struggle is itself where much of the learning happens.

The team is bringing HaLLMos into advanced undergraduate courses in linear algebra, real analysis and topology, after using it in introductory proof classes. An $814,000 grant from the AI for Math Fund, supported by Renaissance Philanthropy and XTX Markets, will pay for that expansion. The grant will also fund a fellowship program with roughly 40 mathematicians, including faculty, postdoctoral researchers and graduate students from across the country. These fellows will help write examples of proofs paired with expert feedback so the AI can learn what useful feedback looks like in each field. Nearly 40,000 student proofs have already been submitted to the tool.

Vincent Vatter, a professor in UF's Department of Mathematics, leads the project. He said that removing all the struggle also removes much of the learning, and that instructors lack the time to give students as much feedback as they need. Vatter said the tool is designed to help students see weaknesses in their reasoning and fix them, rather than simply producing answers. He added that he uses HaLLMos in his own teaching so students can test proofs and revise them before final submission. Co-investigators named in the release are Sarah Sword of Education Development Center, Jay Pantone of Marquette University and Ryota Matsuura of St. Olaf College.

The release places the work against a broader debate about AI in education, noting that leading AI labs are now solving famous open problems in mathematics. The project builds on earlier work supported by the National Science Foundation. HaLLMos is freely available to students and instructors at hallmos.com, where students can practice writing proofs and get immediate feedback, and instructors can create exercises for their courses. The release does not describe any further results or timelines beyond the planned expansion into advanced courses.

stories.Headline: Political ads made with AI break into the midterms campaign
stories.Summary:
Political ads made with artificial intelligence have spread through the 2026 midterm campaign in the United States, according to a count by the Wesleyan Media Project, a university research lab that tracks political advertising. The lab has identified more than 200 such ads, and Travis Ridout, one of its directors, said new ones are being added almost every day. One example cited is an ad from the campaign of Ken Paxton, the Republican state attorney general running against James Talarico for the U.S. Senate in Texas, which shows Talarico apparently rewriting Genesis in a scene that is clearly implausible. A notice at the bottom of the screen says some of the content was generated with artificial intelligence.

The lab estimated spending on these ads at about $80 million in early September and, a month later, said the total had passed $100 million. That is a small share of overall campaign ad spending, which AdImpact estimated at more than $10 billion this week. Ridout said the ads appear to come mostly from outside groups, such as political action committees, though many campaigns use the tactic. Because the tally is compiled by hand and campaigns do not always disclose AI use, the lab describes it as an approximation, and it excludes unpaid material spread on social media.

No federal law governs AI-generated political ads, although 31 states have their own rules, which vary. Some states require disclosure and three ban certain deepfakes. In Tennessee, a law that took effect on July 1 requires AI ads to carry a notice at the beginning and end, but several candidates in a congressional primary ran ads without one, arguing that the state law did not cover federal races. Attempts to ban deceptive AI ads or require disclosures have not advanced in Congress or at the Federal Election Commission. Ridout said campaigns themselves would likely welcome a national rule, while experts note that regulating political speech raises serious legal problems.

Ridout said he sees few truly deceptive deepfakes, and that many ads are obviously fabricated or labeled as satire, a category that often avoids disclosure requirements. His research team found that most people could tell real ads with deepfakes were made with AI, and an experiment suggested the ads did not reduce trust in political advertising overall, though he cautioned that the test was limited. His main concern is whether voters are affected by such ads even after recognizing they are false. The Texas and Tennessee examples show how the patchwork of rules is already producing disputes, and the most aggressive advertising of the campaign is still ahead.

stories.Headline: TinyFish Breaks Down Agentic Search Architecture for Production AI Agents
stories.Summary:
TinyFish, a company that provides web infrastructure for AI agents, has published two technical guides on agentic search architecture for production systems, reported by MarkTechPost on October 23, 2026. The guides address why an AI search agent that works in a demo can fail under real workloads, such as when retrieval returns incomplete evidence, retries repeat unsuccessful actions, or execution exceeds time and cost limits. One guide defines a production architecture, and the other shares lessons from building a deep research system. Together they explain how an autonomous search agent can plan retrieval, evaluate evidence, handle failures, and separate model reasoning from deterministic execution.

TinyFish describes its system as built on four web primitives, called TinySearch, TinyFetch, TinyBrowser, and TinyAgent, operating through a seven-phase control loop around the base model. The loop begins by turning a goal into an evidence contract that sets required fields, sources, freshness, and completion rules, then plans retrieval and chooses a first route. The agent treats search results as candidates until page content arrives, labels evidence as sufficient, incomplete, conflicting, inaccessible, or budget exhausted, and then recovers, escalates, or stops with a validated status. On the OpenBenchmarks coding tasks, TinyFish reports a 79.0% completion rate and the lowest median task cost of $0.050 and token footprint. The architecture draws on a February 2026 preprint that separates reasoning from execution through typed tool interfaces and sets caps on tokens, execution time, cost, and tool invocations.

The guides place responsibility for the design with TinyFish, which says that rigid control loops, failure-specific retries, and unified reasoning work better than standalone planners. The architecture assigns the model to reasoning while the surrounding application keeps ownership of state, tool execution, evidence handling, runtime policies, and output validation. The guides also note that escalation is not always the right fix, since weak results call for a better query and conflicting sources call for stronger evidence. Routing should follow the information gap rather than a fixed ladder, with search used when the source location is unknown, fetch used when a URL is known and readable, and the browser used when the app must control page actions.

The architecture builds on prior research that the guides cite to justify specific design choices. One cited problem is the lost-in-retrieval issue described in ChainRAG at ACL 2025, where key entities disappear during multi-hop question decomposition. The guides also cite Search-R1, which showed that models can learn to generate additional search queries during reasoning when earlier retrieval falls short, and which beat RAG baselines by 41% on Qwen2.5-7B and 20% on Qwen2.5-3B across seven QA datasets. These references support the seven-phase loop's emphasis on recovering from incomplete retrieval instead of accepting the first answer. The articles present the design as a response to failures seen in production, not as a finished solution for every case.
