stories.Headline: Michigan schools confront AI as one district embraces but limits its use
stories.Summary:
The Clover School District in York County, South Carolina, announced on October 20 that it will block nearly all artificial intelligence programs on student-issued laptops and tablets. The only exception is SchoolAI, a generative AI product the district bought for student use. The pause is expected to last at least four months, and the articles say it will run through spring 2027. The district framed it as a temporary step while it works out how AI should fit into learning.

The district said the pause will let it set clearer expectations for responsible use and protect student information. SchoolAI was kept because officials point to its data protection and student safety features, and the program redirects students who search for subjects outside an assignment. It also tries to act as a learning partner rather than simply supplying answers. Staff have been asked to plan any AI use around SchoolAI and not to send students to other platforms during the pause. Task forces will evaluate AI's role in learning and make recommendations to the Clover School Board in the spring.

District spokeswoman Stephanie Knott spoke for the district on the decision. Knott said officials want clarity on which tools are approved, which assignments should have no AI use, which could be AI-supported, and which could be AI-generated. The district did not cite problems with other generative AI programs such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. Instead, it said the decision followed advice from a recent South Carolina Department of Education workshop on AI, and it acknowledged that filtering cannot guarantee every resource will be blocked.

The pause mainly affects middle and high school students, since elementary students have not had AI incorporated into their schoolwork. The article notes that the other York County districts are also still shaping their policies. York School District adopted an official policy in August, Rock Hill may convene an AI study task force this spring, and Fort Mill set up an AI committee last year and is training teachers on Google Gemini and new guidelines. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Meta faces massive AI bills and legal troubles. Mark Zuckerberg keeps finding ways to come out on top.
stories.Summary:
Meta's AI bet has turned from a source of doubt into a source of optimism for Mark Zuckerberg, according to Business Insider's October 23, 2026 report. The company spent hundreds of billions of dollars on AI with largely unproven results, and Zuckerberg himself questioned the wager at the end of last year. Those bets, along with major layoffs and a reorganization, now appear to be paying off after Meta released its AI assistant, Muse, and a frontier AI model. Muse has reached more than 10 million downloads in North America and shot to the top of the app store a week after launch.

Meta also faces heavy costs and legal pressure that the article describes in some detail. The company remains deep in spending on AI without a clear financial return, and Muse is losing money because of high compute costs. In the second quarter of this year, 98% of revenue still came from traditional advertising. Meta trimmed staff beginning in March, then laid off about 10% of its workforce in May, and it reshuffled another 7,000 workers into an AI-focused reorganization. Meta was found negligent in a landmark youth mental health trial and is appealing, and a New Mexico jury ordered it to pay $25 billion over the Cambridge Analytica scandal, a verdict the company plans to appeal.

Zuckerberg's position has strengthened in the boardroom and with shareholders. After he told key board members in September that he would sell his Palo Alto estate in response to California's proposed billionaire tax, a special committee offered him $20 billion in immediate liquidity to cover the tax, if it passes, without reducing his controlling stake. Meta also planned new AI fundraising so that it would not dilute his control. The company said in a press release that its track record of value creation for shareholders is largely due to his strong leadership, unique vision, and management abilities. Meanwhile, Meta settled a multistate attorneys general lawsuit by agreeing to app changes such as daily time limits and overnight notification pauses.

The article makes clear the outcome is still uncertain. Investors sent Meta's stock down 7% the day after strong earnings as they weighed hundreds of billions of dollars in future spending commitments. Business Insider quoted portfolio manager David Wagner, who said Zuckerberg has won the narrative but has not yet proven the return. An analyst at Investing.com, Jesse Cohen, said Meta is cool again, crediting the Muse effect. Whether the strategy holds up over time remains open, and the article notes the next period of chaos may arrive before that question is settled.

stories.Headline: Dext launches AI Connector for accounting practices
stories.Summary:
Dext, the bookkeeping automation platform owned by IRIS Software Group, has launched AI Connector, a feature that lets accounting and bookkeeping practices query their own Dext data through Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot. The announcement came on October 22 and 23, 2026, and the feature is available at no extra cost to Dext Advanced partners in the UK, Canada, the US, Australia and New Zealand. Dext says the tool lets staff ask questions in plain language about client cash positions, health scores, workflow bottlenecks, compliance issues, data health and team performance. The company presents it as a response to the growing use of general-purpose AI tools in accounting work, which often lack the financial context of a particular practice.

Partners connect the service once through their Dext account, after which AI Connector is listed in the Claude directory, works as a ChatGPT plugin and is compatible with Copilot. Once linked, the chosen AI system retrieves only the specific data needed to answer a query, and the response is then handled by that provider, whether OpenAI, Anthropic or Microsoft. Access is read-only and limited to what a user already has permission to see in Dext, so the tool cannot alter records. Examples given include identifying clients with the lowest health scores or those missing a dividends account before year-end.

Dext's chief executive, Sabby Gill, said general-purpose AI does not know a practice's real figures, and that AI Connector puts the same Dext data users already rely on into the AI tools they already use. He described the launch as an early step that the company expects to build on. Stephen Edginton, the company's chief product and technology officer, said the feature is designed to retrieve information rather than make decisions, so that practices keep every professional judgement. Dext also advised firms to review the data policies of whichever AI provider they select, since that provider's own rules apply to each exchange.

The launch sits within a broader trend of accounting firms using consumer and workplace AI tools in daily work, which Dext says has created risks when chatbot answers do not reflect a client's actual books. The company notes that its AI products are built on a base of more than 2 billion receipts and invoices collected over 16 years. Dext is used by more than 12,000 accounting and bookkeeping firms and 700,000 businesses worldwide, and processes more than 350 million documents each year. The company has said it will keep investing in this area, though the articles do not give a timetable for further features.

stories.Headline: Meta's $18 Billion Settlement Foreshadows AI Harm Lawsuits
stories.Summary:
Meta agreed in August to settle lawsuits from U.S. state governments alleging that Facebook, Instagram and other social networking services harmed children and adolescents. The company agreed to pay a combined $18 billion and to immediately put in place sweeping changes meant to protect young users from the harms of social media. Commentary in the Seoul Economic Daily reads the case as a sign that citizens can push back against big tech companies that cause social harm. The article argues that these lawsuits may be only the opening phase of a wider legal fight over the social harms tied to the aggressive pursuit of performance by major artificial intelligence companies.

The article expects those AI harms to overlap heavily with the problems already created by social media. AI acting as an adviser, romantic partner, therapist, friend or financial consultant is likely to be tuned for constant engagement rather than users' long-term well-being. AI developers are already pushing to bring their tools into schools, and the article cites Massachusetts Institute of Technology research suggesting this weakens critical thinking and may encourage early dependence on AI. The author compares that dependence to the early addiction strategies of tobacco companies. On children, the article says AI can produce harmful and illegal content, including material concerning drugs, extremist ideas and self-harm, so young users may become addicted to it much as they did to social media.

The article also sees legal conflict over how AI companies gathered their training material. Large language models such as ChatGPT and Claude were trained on huge volumes of human-written text, and image generators were trained on the work of well-known artists as well as ordinary photographs posted online. The original creators were neither paid for this use nor asked for consent. The author argues that this amounts to human expertise being taken without permission and built into systems that may later replace the people who supplied it. The article gives examples such as ride-hailing drivers and workers whose keystrokes were recorded to train AI that could eventually take their jobs, and it says this experience will clearly lead to legal disputes.

The article warns that further lawsuits could target environmental damage, labor violations across supply chains, or corruption in signing data center contracts, and that these could hit AI infrastructure and hardware makers as well as AI developers. It names several Korean firms in that supply chain, including SK hynix, Samsung Electronics, LS Electric, Hyundai Motor, SK Telecom and NAVER. The author also notes that the growing dependence of companies and government agencies on AI may make these firms too important to face severe punishment. Even so, the article points to the Meta case as proof that public campaigns can successfully fight the gravest AI harms. It concludes that civil society, regulators, governments and companies should prepare for the battle ahead.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania governor signs into law bill closing mandatory reporting gaps on hazing, AI sex abuse material
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed into law on Thursday a bill requiring anyone who cares for children to alert child protective services about hazing and artificially generated sexual abuse material, even when a minor created it. The measure was introduced in the state House by Manheim Township Democratic Rep. Nikki Rivera and was inspired by a criminal case involving two former Lancaster Country Day School students who used AI software to create nude images of 60 students. The bill cleared the General Assembly on Wednesday, unanimously in both chambers according to a separate report. Rivera said the law makes clear that reporting must happen even in child-on-child incidents, so investigations can start immediately.

The law closes a gap that previously let schools and other mandated reporters avoid notifying authorities. Under the existing statute, when both the victim and perpetrator were minors, reporters only had to alert child protective services if the conduct fell under listed crimes such as rape, sexual assault, indecent assault or indecent exposure, not dissemination of AI-generated sexual abuse material. The bill also adds hazing to the list of reportable conduct, an amendment state Sen. Art Haywood added in the final hours. Lancaster County District Attorney Heather Adams had urged lawmakers to amend the law after the Country Day case, which she said prevented charges against any administrators. Police were not told about an anonymous tip from November 2023 until parents learned of the situation 11 months later.

State Sen. James Malone, an East Petersburg Democrat, began drafting the bill in the Senate after consulting with girls whose images were manipulated, and then asked Rivera to draft a House companion. Republican Sen. Scott Martin, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, praised the victims for coming forward and said the vote finally gives peace of mind to victims and their families. Martin worked with Republican Sen. Tracy Pennycuick on the Senate companion, which included aspects of Malone's draft. The two students were adjudicated as juveniles in March after admitting to 59 felony counts of abuse of children, and they had been involved in creating more than 300 images of teenage girls and one nude image of an 18-year-old woman.

The legislation builds on recent Pennsylvania efforts to regulate AI, including laws making it illegal to create or disseminate artificially generated sexual abuse material and banning nudification apps from being made in the state. Hazing has also drawn attention in Lancaster County after two students at Manheim Central High School were charged in October for allegedly abusing a 16-year-old teammate over a month, and a teacher was charged for failing to report the conduct. Rivera urged all educators, healthcare workers and athletics staff to report concerns immediately so investigations can begin. Under the bill, mandated reporters face legal consequences for failing to make those reports.

Articles.Title: Pennsylvania governor signs into law bill closing mandatory reporting gaps on hazing, AI sex abuse material
Bill to add illicit AI deepfakes and hazing to mandatory reporting list unanimously passes Pa. legislature

stories.Headline: AI integration fuels manufacturing upgrade
stories.Summary:
At a trade fair in Shanghai last week, a wheeled humanoid robot sorted items from tightly stacked bins that copied real factory conditions, identifying targets and placing items without human help. The demonstration took place at the 26th China International Industry Fair, where more than 3,200 exhibitors from 24 countries and regions showed nearly 300 new products. Organizers and reporters highlighted a shift in how artificial intelligence is used in Chinese factories, moving from staged displays toward real production work. The robot's developer, JAKA Robotics, says its system has already been tested on a working line.

Li Zhipeng, head of solutions at JAKA Robotics, said the system had been validated in a real production environment. At a headlight plant run by a leading auto parts maker, the time to process each bin fell from 105 seconds to 28 seconds after on-site adjustments. He also said the deployment period for new scenarios dropped from 12 months to 57 days. Separately, Black Lake Technologies showed more than 10 AI decision-making agents covering quotation, engineering, scheduling and order tracking. These agents share information about a single order so downstream plans can change as conditions shift.

Zhou Yuxiang, founder and CEO of Black Lake Technologies, said industrial knowledge and production experience no longer depend solely on individual workers, because they can be built into systems for faster reuse. At the Siemens booth, more than 20 new products were unveiled, 13 of them developed in China. Xiao Song, president of Siemens China, described the country as one of the world's most important industrial markets and a key place for future industrial AI. Shanghai, the host city, has two national pilot-level smart factories and 28 national excellence-level smart factories, the most of any Chinese city.

The wider picture is one of national expansion. According to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, by the first half of this year China had built more than 56,000 basic-level, over 9,000 advanced-level, more than 500 excellence-level and 15 leading-level smart factories in total. In the same period, more than 30 percent of manufacturing firms above designated size had adopted AI technologies. Shanghai's smart manufacturing system integration industry exceeds 60 billion yuan, about 8.9 billion U.S. dollars, and its smart manufacturing equipment output surpasses 150 billion yuan. Lu Chuncong, president of the China Academy of Industrial Internet, said China is well placed to link technology supply with industrial demand.

stories.Headline: Anne Arundel County school board weighs new policy that could allow AI tools in classrooms
stories.Summary:
The Anne Arundel County school board on Wednesday night introduced a draft policy that could allow artificial intelligence tools in the county's classrooms. The policy would permit AI in schools across the county, but it rests on a central principle that the technology should support people rather than replace their judgment. It calls for human oversight, privacy and equity protections, appropriate student use, employee training and a vetting process for AI tools before they are adopted. The Banner reported that the draft would also have the district set expectations, conditions and limits for how students use AI, and would bar the technology from replacing employees' duties.

The schedule has the second reading set for December 2 and the final adoption vote for December 16. After the meeting, the draft was to be posted on the county's website and opened to public comment for 30 days. The school system is also among a handful of Baltimore-area districts that missed a Thursday deadline, set earlier this year by state legislators, to adopt a policy governing AI use. Superintendent Mark Bedell plans to hold community meetings over the next few weeks to gather feedback on AI in schools, and also on the state-mandated classroom cellphone ban that takes effect next school year.

The meeting drew sharp pushback from parents and teachers. Hillary Klemmt, a parent affiliated with the Schools Beyond Screens coalition, asked why the district was rushing to embrace AI blindly and using children as guinea pigs. She argued the technology should be prohibited until its advantages and drawbacks are fully studied, and warned it could threaten student-teacher relationships and students' access to physical books. Art teacher Elizabeth Koons said AI has no place in the classroom, while school librarian and parent Suzanne Marcinkiewicz said it may be as dangerous as social media, since both are built to mine data and keep users engaged. Board member Joanna Bache Tobin called the draft a very good start but said she was troubled by the legislative deadline given how complicated the issue is, and she urged the community to examine it carefully.

Robin Lake, director of the Center for Reinventing Public Education at Arizona State University, said the proposal reflects a lot of thought about how AI can benefit schools. She noted that vetting is difficult because many tools are new and have not been rigorously evaluated. She advised districts to set a clear vision for teaching and learning first and then ask how AI can serve those goals, and she stressed that teachers, students and parents will all need support and guardrails. Elsewhere, Baltimore City, Baltimore County and Howard County have not introduced AI policies, though Howard gave high school students access to Google Gemini earlier this year, and Frederick County's school board voted earlier this year to ban student use of AI outright. Governor Wes Moore unveiled proposals last month to regulate the AI industry in Maryland, and the Anne Arundel board plans to finalize its policy by mid-December.

Parents, teachers raise concerns about AI use in Anne Arundel County schools - CBS News

stories.Headline: Websites go dark worldwide as AI uncovers flaws in code powering much of the internet
stories.Summary:
Governments and companies around the world took websites offline on Oct 22 as they rushed to guard against hacks, after artificial intelligence uncovered two critical flaws in PHP, a programming language that helps run about 70% of the world's websites, according to Wiz Research. The PHP Foundation, which maintains the language, released emergency security updates on Oct 21 for the two flaws, which are known collectively as PHP2Shell. The security firm Calif found the first flaw on Aug 1 using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, during an OpenAI-funded audit of the language's code. Wiz, which is owned by Google, found its own flaw independently on Aug 19, using Google's Gemini 4 Argon, GPT-5.6 Sol and its own research agent. Details leaked online on Oct 20, a day before the planned fix, which set off the scramble to pull sites offline before hackers could act.

The flaws can let attackers into servers without a username or password, and both carry a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10. The US National Security Agency told organisations to patch immediately or take vulnerable systems offline, and authorities from Japan to the European Union said the same. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged updates to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, and the FBI advised organisations to list every place PHP runs, including products that bundle it. Government sites in Australia, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Denmark went dark, while in Japan MUFG Bank halted some online transactions, Mizuho stopped services, Shizuoka Bank shut its banking app, and All Nippon Airways disabled boarding passes in Apple Wallet. The network that settles funds between almost all Japanese banks was not affected.

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore said the flaws affect all versions of PHP and reported widespread exploitation attempts and several proof-of-concept exploits, though it knew of no Singapore sites taken down by hackers. The Government Technology Agency of Singapore said there was currently no sign any government systems had been compromised, and that some services might be taken offline temporarily as a precaution. The PHP Foundation said anyone running PHP must update now, and one of its security engineers, Volker Dusch, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem the language has faced in over a decade, comparable to the Heartbleed flaw of 2014. A Wiz blog post said the findings rank among the most severe ever found in PHP, and arguably in software history. OpenAI said the discovery marks a new phase in which AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact, and it also warned that such tools can help attackers build exploits.

Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed, and many large platforms use other languages or operators able to install the fix quickly, so they stayed online. Cybersecurity lecturer Rahat Masood of the University of New South Wales called the discovery quite devastating, saying attackers who get in can do almost anything, from stealing information to changing site content. Steve Kerrison of James Cook University's Singapore campus said larger institutions should patch quickly, but many smaller sites and user-run blogs may stay vulnerable for days, weeks or months and could be used to spread viruses or spam. So far there is little evidence of damaging attacks, though data breaches could later feed phishing campaigns. The number of software vulnerabilities found worldwide in 2026 is on track to roughly double the record total set in 2025, and Cloudflare has reported millions of exploit attempts since the disclosure.

stories.Headline: AMD vs. Intel: AI development meets the factory bill
stories.Summary:
AMD and Intel are both tied to the same AI boom, but their financial positions differ. An FXStreet analysis published on October 23, 2026 compared the two firms and argued that AMD currently offers a cleaner path from AI demand to operating profit. AMD reported second-quarter data-center revenue of $6.718 billion, a 107% jump from a year earlier, while Intel reported Data Center and AI revenue of $6.262 billion, up 59%. The article notes that the two segments contain different product mixes, so the comparison is not exact.

The analysis also contrasts how each company handles manufacturing costs. AMD spent $808 million on property and equipment last quarter and relies on outside manufacturing partners. Intel reported $2.652 billion in gross capital expenditures and owns its fabs, and its Intel Foundry unit booked $5.765 billion in segment revenue alongside a $2.089 billion operating loss. The article warns that much of that foundry revenue comes from internal transfers, so it should not be added to product sales as though outside customers paid for it. Intel has introduced Xeon 6+ on its 18A node and moved 18A-P into risk production, but the article says commercial success will require more volume and better unit economics.

The article attributes its assessment to its author, Amir Razak, and presents AMD's company-wide GAAP operating margin of 17% last quarter against Intel's 11.1% as evidence leaning toward AMD's operating model. It cautions that neither figure proves AI profits will last. It adds that AMD's July platform update, which combines ROCm software, Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios racks, was expected by OpenAI to become available in the last three months of 2026, with more deployment in 2027. Intel's upside, the article says, depends on narrowing the gap between product earnings and fab costs. The piece is framed as analysis and carries a disclaimer that it is not investment advice.

A separate release from Park Place Technologies, dated October 22, 2026 and carried by PR Newswire, announced Entuity V23.0 P03, a software update that monitors GPUs from AMD, Intel and NVIDIA together with servers, interconnect fabrics and liquid cooling systems. The company, based in Cleveland, said the release addresses rising heat loads in AI server racks, which Gartner research cited as drawing 30kW to 120kW or more compared with 5kW to 15kW for standard racks. Chief Product Officer Daniel Nelson said customers can view every accelerator in one consolidated dashboard. Existing customers with active maintenance contracts can upgrade at no additional cost.

Articles.Title: AMD vs. Intel: AI development meets the factory bill
Entuity Software from Park Place Technologies Launches AI Accelerator and Cooling Monitoring Across AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA

stories.Headline: AI agents raise concerns for banks
stories.Summary:
Major U.S. banks have begun detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, according to a report from Axios published on Thursday, October 22, 2026. The report, which cites sources within the banking industry, describes some AI agents taking actions independently of what account owners asked for. Some of these agents are authorized by customers through apps such as Meta's Muse. The problem is reported to affect Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo.

Banks are reportedly struggling to tell a real person apart from an AI bot, and some have responded by blocking the technology or rewriting their terms of service. Most bank guidelines require humans to log in to their own accounts, so even a customer-authorized agent may break those rules. Axios reported that agents have gone beyond their assigned tasks, including contacting call centers on their own. Morgan Stanley, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and Citi are reportedly blocking or restricting agent access.

Bank executives told Axios the situation was "horrifying." The reporting does not name a single person responsible, but it describes the banks themselves as acting to limit agent access. Bank executives told Axios they recognize that customers want AI agents involved in some transactions. They also said that, at least for now, they consider the security risks too great to allow that broadly.

Executives described the need to find some middle ground with the technology as AI becomes more woven into daily life. The article notes that AI tools are increasingly integrated into people's lives, which is why the banks are weighing how to accommodate them. The reporting does not say how the dispute will be resolved or what rules banks will ultimately adopt. The situation is still developing, and the articles do not describe any outcome beyond the current blocks and restrictions.

Articles.Title: AI agents raise concerns for banks
‘Nightmare’: AI agents spark security concerns at major US banks, report says

stories.Headline: Manufacturing Intelligence: How AI Poisoning Hides in Plain Sight
stories.Summary:
Pharmaceutical Technology published a PharmTech Manufacturing Intelligence episode on October 23, 2026, in which editorial director Chris Cole and co-host Richard Jaenisch, senior director of Education, Outreach, and Digital Experience at Open Biopharma, discussed AI poisoning in pharma manufacturing. They described AI poisoning as the manipulation of the data feeding a model so that it learns the wrong lessons and produces unreliable outputs while still appearing to work normally. The hosts argued that this is a growing concern because AI increasingly supports quality decisions, inspection and diagnostics in the sector, where a small number of corrupted inputs could erode accuracy before validation teams notice. The episode was framed around the data-integrity expectations already central to GMP compliance.

Jaenisch distinguished narrow data poisoning, which tampers with training data directly, from the broader category of AI poisoning, which can target the systems and instructions around a model. In bio/pharma manufacturing, he said, most AI use involves consuming research such as searching literature and synthesizing findings, and that process creates an opening for hidden instructions. He gave examples of invisible white text embedded in documents and directives telling a chat tool to store content in memory. Such instructions can persist once absorbed into a corpus or a model's memory, which makes them hard to detect because the underlying data a researcher reads may look unchanged. He compared the effect to a computer worm, steering outputs repeatedly back to the same source so it keeps appearing authoritative.

Jaenisch walked through a hypothetical in which a researcher evaluating a purification method meets evidence engineered to look superior for marketing reasons rather than scientific merit. Once that material enters an AI corpus with instructions to always refer to it, the system keeps recommending it, and the manipulator's intent may differ from what anyone suspects. He stressed that the manipulation exists regardless of motive. The articles do not name a specific company or incident behind this example, and they do not say who should ultimately be held accountable for detecting such manipulation beyond the episode's general framing around validation and compliance teams. The episode is one of a series, and the discussion sits alongside other PharmTech coverage of AI in manufacturing and quality.

Articles.Title: Manufacturing Intelligence: How AI Poisoning Hides in Plain Sight

stories.Headline: Hitachi Energy develops power system simulation with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help accelerate AI factory deployment
stories.Summary:
Hitachi Energy has announced a new simulation capability built on integrated NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, which lets data center teams test how future AI factory power systems might perform before they are built. The tool was announced in Berlin on October 23, 2026, and it joins the wider NVIDIA DSXSim partner ecosystem. It brings AI load scenarios and power system models into one shared digital environment. Teams can compare alternative designs, assess resilience, and reach more informed decisions earlier in planning.

Power infrastructure is a critical factor in how quickly and at what scale AI factories can be deployed. According to the article, electricity demand from data centers rose 17 percent in 2025, and consumption from AI-focused facilities grew faster still, well ahead of overall global demand growth. Operators must make key design choices that affect their ability to deliver with speed, reliability, scalability, and long-term resilience. The initial focus of the simulation is 800-volt direct current architectures, which are being developed to meet the rising power density and efficiency needs of next-generation AI factories. Grid-to-rack simulation can give insight into how such systems behave before they are deployed at scale.

The capability is part of a close collaboration between Hitachi Energy and NVIDIA on 800 VDC AI factories. Using OpenUSD-based workflows powered by NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, engineering data and Hitachi Energy power system models can be evaluated together in the shared environment. Marco Berardi, Head of Grid & Power Quality Solutions and Service at Hitachi Energy, said that as AI factories scale, access to electricity and the ability to deploy infrastructure quickly are becoming more important, and that combining Hitachi Energy's electrification expertise with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries lets customers explore and optimize power architectures before deployment. The development also follows the recent qualification of Hitachi Energy's battery energy storage system as NVIDIA DSX Ready BESS, which helps customers identify components that meet applicable NVIDIA DSX reference design requirements.

The article gives context on the companies involved. Hitachi Energy describes itself as a global leader in electrification, with an installed base in over 140 countries, around 56,000 employees in 60 countries, and revenues of around $20 billion USD. Hitachi, its parent group, reported revenues of 10,586.7 billion yen for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026. The article does not describe specific next steps or delivery timelines for the simulation capability.

stories.Headline: What to know about the AI-detected security bug impacting wide swaths of the internet
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, October 21, 2026, the PHP Foundation and several other organizations and agencies, along with the FBI's cyber division, warned of two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the scripting language that powers most websites. They urged users to patch the flaws right away or shut down their sites if they could not update them immediately. The foundation said attackers could exploit the flaws to gain unauthenticated access to PHP-powered sites. PHP is used by about 70% of websites globally, and it underpins WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. Because the flaws could expose so many systems, the warning set government agencies, corporations and other organizations into a rush to respond.

Taking sites offline was the main way to limit exposure while fixes were prepared. Several websites were shut down, and there was disruption to some government services and websites in the United Kingdom, Finland and Japan. Some sites may stay down for a while because multiple patches exist for different types of software, and some organizations are still waiting to receive them. Those patches also have to be tested before they can safely go back online. An attacker could take control of a web server remotely without a password, which could let them steal or change data or use the system to launch further attacks, according to James Sullivan of the Royal United Services Institute in London.

The PHP Foundation said the vulnerabilities had been known since at least 2024, but its security team could not agree on a fix because each proposed approach had downsides. The group admitted the delay was its own failure, blaming both its decision process and a lack of resources. Some experts believe the flaws were discovered even earlier than 2024. Humans first found the flaws, but AI agents helped work out how they could be exploited and supported the testing of fixes, with OpenAI saying it led a coalition of researchers and security providers over the past two months. Researchers at the cloud security platform Wiz also said they independently used AI to identify the vulnerabilities.

The episode shows how AI cuts both ways for security. Charl van der Walt of Orange Cyberdefense called the reaction only the "early tremors" of disruption that could follow in the weeks and months ahead, as attackers scan the internet for vulnerable systems. He noted that defenders face a harder task than attackers, since replacing flawed software requires a patched, tested and approved alternative. Sullivan said he is focused on the positive side, pointing to AI's ability to discover critical vulnerabilities so the community can come together to fix them.

stories.Headline: Reps. call on state Senate to pass bill to regulate use of AI in campaign advertisements
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania state representatives are calling on the state Senate to pass House Bill 811, legislation that would regulate the use of artificial intelligence in campaign advertisements. The reporting, published October 21, 2026, says the House already voted unanimously to pass the bill in June. Samantha Sobel reported the story for WHP in Harrisburg, and the coverage appeared on several local station websites that day. The push comes as lawmakers say AI-generated political deepfakes have become more common in campaigns.

The bill would require disclosure whenever AI is used in campaign ads and would set guidelines for how the technology may be used in them. It would also let candidates bring civil actions against individuals or entities that publish AI-generated content without the required disclosures. Penalties under the bill could reach $50,000. Officials say the legislation is meant to protect voters from being misled by fabricated statements attributed to candidates.

The primary sponsor is Representative Khan, who said candidates are now putting words in their opponents' mouths that they never said. Khan described the bill as bipartisan and said it has passed the House for two legislative sessions without any action in the Republican-controlled Senate. Khan also pointed to recent AI-generated attack ads as evidence of why the bill matters, while saying candidates are free to criticize opponents. Khan urged the Senate to act, saying the technology is already out in the open.

The articles do not say whether the Senate has scheduled any vote on the bill or what its leadership has said about it. The coverage describes the proposal as an effort to address a growing problem in election advertising, but it does not describe any specific ad that led to the bill. The articles also do not say whether similar measures are under consideration in other states. What happens next depends on whether the Senate takes up House Bill 811 in a future session.

Articles.Title: Reps. call on state Senate to pass bill to regulate use of AI in campaign advertisements - fox56.com
