stories.Headline: AI now helps Australians choose brands, study finds
stories.Summary:
A research report from the Australian Centre for AI in Marketing, published on 22 October 2026, argues that brands must now win the approval of both artificial intelligence systems and consumers. The study, called The Navigators' AI Brandscape 2026, surveyed 1,736 Australians and found that 39 per cent had used generative AI to help choose a brand, product or service. The report says the early stage of the customer journey is becoming harder for marketers to see, because more people use AI tools to research purchases before they buy. As a result, a brand can be ruled out before the customer ever makes a final choice.

The research also shows that consumers are cautious about letting AI take full control. Just 11 per cent of respondents said they would allow AI to make a purchase decision, even for low-stakes products. The report describes a gap between using AI for research and handing it decision-making power, and it urges marketers to understand which tasks people are willing to delegate. ACAM's Customer Delegation Framework asks four questions: whether AI can do the job, whether it is worth using, whether the customer stays in charge, and whether such use is socially normal. Customers are more willing to hand over tasks when AI is clearly useful and convenient, while worries about control, trust and social acceptance hold back wider use.

Louise Cummins, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of ACAM, said that brands now have to be chosen twice, first by a customer's AI and then by the customer. She warned that a brand missing from the AI's shortlist may never get the chance to make its case. Cummins said marketers need to know what information AI uses to make recommendations and what earns customer trust. Duncan Egan, Vice President of Enterprise Marketing for Asia Pacific and Japan at Adobe, which supported the report, said teams should focus on orchestrating connected experiences rather than only creating campaigns. Egan added that people should remain in control of strategy, brand and the customer relationship.

The report sets this shift against a gap in readiness. Its 2026 AI in Marketing Benchmark, conducted with Kantar, found that 83 per cent of participating Australian organisations sat at levels one to three of ACAM's six-level maturity scale, and none reached levels five or six. Separate research from Twilio and YouGov, cited in the report, found that 78 per cent of people had used AI-powered customer service but only 39 per cent were satisfied, and 84 per cent wanted an easy way to reach a person. The publication, the third in ACAM's research programme, includes a 90-day plan for marketing leaders and examples from Budget Direct, ANZ, Telstra and Woolworths.

Articles.Title: AI now helps Australians choose brands, study finds - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: TAPP、Google Cloud Agentic AI Summit '26 Fall
stories.Summary:
Cognizant and Google Cloud announced on October 19, 2026, an expansion of their partnership to accelerate the adoption of agentic AI. They launched a new Gemini Frontier Capability Group, backed by more than 18,000 dedicated Cognizant associates. The group pairs Google Cloud’s full-stack, enterprise-ready AI platform with Cognizant’s domain, industry, and engineering expertise. It builds on the momentum created by Cognizant’s dedicated Gemini practice launched in April 2026.

The new group is designed to bridge the path from pilot to production, helping enterprises safely deploy resilient, enterprise-grade agents that can drive measurable business value. It will initially concentrate on legacy modernization, developer experience, autonomous business process agentification, and frontier cyber defense. The group plans to deploy standardized, security-first agentic architecture built on the Model Context Protocol and fortified by Google Cloud’s Model Armor. These frameworks are expected to power solutions including Cognizant’s Catalog Support Agent for retail, the Neuro San-orchestrated Healthcare Agentic Marketplace, and multi-agent Order-to-Cash workflows for manufacturing. Cognizant is also applying Gemini internally, with plans to deploy it to 100,000 associates this year and scale up to 200,000.

Ravi Kumar S, CEO of Cognizant, said the group lets the company’s best frontier engineering talent focus entirely on getting frontier AI into production for clients. He noted that the Build with Gemini workshop gave over 55,000 associates direct experience and tangible skills on the advanced AI platform. Thomas Kurian, chief executive officer of Google Cloud, said deploying AI agents at scale requires trusted partners with deep architectural and integration expertise. He added that Cognizant’s dedicated group and skilling initiative for tens of thousands of engineers will help joint customers accelerate adoption of autonomous agents throughout the enterprise.

The Build with Gemini workshop was completed by more than 55,000 Cognizant associates, making it the largest single Gemini partner workshop held to date. One early proof point showed that by integrating Gemini AI models across its software development lifecycle, Cognizant helped a leading retailer achieve a 40 percent increase in developer productivity, reduce time-to-market by 30 percent, and realize a 35 percent cost savings. The announcement was made from Teaneck, New Jersey, and Sunnyvale, California. The articles do not specify further next steps beyond the group’s initial focus areas and the planned scaling of Gemini to more Cognizant associates.

stories.Headline: Engineering for scale without boundaries: Architecting the AI-native telecom network - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
This article is an opinion piece rather than a news report, so there is no breaking event to narrate, but I can write it as a summary following the requested structure. Indian telecom operators face a sharp rise in data demand as artificial intelligence moves deeper into their networks. The author argues they must redesign physical infrastructure so capacity can grow in modular steps that match real customer needs. Nokia's Mobile Broadband Index puts average monthly mobile data use above 31 GB per user, with total traffic above 27 exabytes a month. Ericsson's June 2026 Mobility Report expects per-user consumption to nearly double within five years.

The piece calls for power and cooling systems that can scale as demand rises, rather than being forecast to an exact peak. It describes higher-voltage DC power distribution as a strategy to improve efficiency and support denser loads, while acknowledging stricter safety rules, limited skilled labour, and higher upfront costs. Thermal designs should allow air and liquid cooling to coexist, so sites do not become dead ends as loads increase. Serviceability is also stressed, with components that generalist technicians can swap, remote monitoring that flags problems early, and digital twins to test designs before capital is committed.

The article is written by A.S. Prasad, Vice President of Product Management and Engineering at Vertiv India, and it is published on ETCIO, which notes that the views are the author's alone and do not necessarily reflect its own. The author draws on Vertiv's Frontiers 2026 report, which identifies distributed AI, digital twin-driven design, and higher-voltage DC distribution as defining trends. The author's recommended approach is to pilot these solutions in high-density areas rather than commit to them wholesale. The piece closes by posing three questions operators should be able to answer: whether capacity can be added in modular steps, whether sites can be monitored and serviced without specialist visits, and whether designs can be validated digitally before investment.

stories.Headline: TSMC advances CoPoS packaging at Taoyuan Longtan site
stories.Summary:
TSMC's Longtan Science Park Phase 3 in Taoyuan is restarting after nearly three years of delays. Taiwan's National Development Council approved the development plan for the site on September 17, 2026. The report, published by Digitimes on October 23, 2026, ties this approval to the company's advancing CoPoS packaging work at the location. The article's visible text is limited, and much of it is navigation, subscription prompts and site boilerplate rather than reporting. Because the body of the story sits behind a paywall, the full details of the packaging plan are not available in the material provided.

The text available says only that the approval and restart mark a change after a long stretch of delay at the Phase 3 site. It does not state the size of the investment, the number of jobs, the production capacity, or the timeline for CoPoS output at Taoyuan. The article's summary gives no figures beyond the September 17 approval date and the three years of delay. Readers should not assume further specifics from the headline alone. Any changes to the site's scope or schedule that the full article may describe are not included in the excerpt provided.

The approval came from Taiwan's National Development Council, which the excerpt names as the body that cleared the development plan. The excerpt does not include any statement from TSMC or from government officials explaining the reasons for the delay or the restart. It also does not say who else, if anyone, has been named as responsible for the earlier setbacks. The site belongs to TSMC, and the report frames the company as the party advancing the packaging work.

Beyond that, the material does not attribute remarks to specific people. The surrounding page shows other recent coverage about TSMC, including reports on wafer price increases for 2027 and talks about possible involvement in Elon Musk's Terafab project, but the excerpt does not connect these stories to the Longtan approval. The available text does not say what comes next for the Phase 3 site or when construction or CoPoS production is expected to begin. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI Memory Boom Is Funding China's Chip Catch-Up
stories.Summary:
Chinese memory chipmakers are closing the gap with their Korean rivals, and industry watchers say the AI memory boom is paying for it. According to a Seoul Economic Daily report published on October 23, 2026, ChangXin Memory Technologies, a Chinese DRAM maker, and Yangtze Memory Technologies, a NAND flash producer, are expanding capacity and moving into each other's main business lines. The report says CXMT is pursuing NAND research while YMTC has started work on DRAM, suggesting both want to become full-line suppliers. The article's author is Seo Jong-gap, and industry watchers quoted in the piece say competition could intensify sharply once China's new fabs reach full operation in 2027 and 2028.

The growth figures are steep. CXMT's preliminary nine-month guidance, released on October 16, implies third-quarter revenue of 114.7 billion to 119.7 billion yuan, roughly seven times the year-earlier figure. Counterpoint Research put CXMT's share of global DRAM revenue at 10 percent in the second quarter, up from 4 percent a year earlier. SemiAnalysis projects CXMT's monthly DRAM wafer capacity will rise from about 350,000 wafers at the end of this year to 500,000 by the end of 2028. YMTC has reached third place globally in NAND shipment share and is targeting a 20 percent share over the long term.

Analysts attribute the windfall to a DRAM supply shortage and price increases driven by AI server investment, and the companies are reinvesting it. YMTC reportedly has 4,796 R&D staff, has spent 14.2 billion yuan on R&D over three years, and holds 5,611 registered invention patents. It is using its Xtacking wafer bonding technology to work around U.S. export controls on advanced chipmaking equipment. The article notes that Samsung Electronics reportedly signed a related patent licensing agreement with YMTC last year. The report also says CXMT's July stock market listing raised a large sum that adds to its investment capacity.

The article cautions that a rising market share does not yet mean the technology gap is closing. CXMT's DDR5 products are reported to carry manufacturing costs per unit of data capacity more than 30 percent higher than those of Korean and U.S. producers. Analysts quoted in the report say the threat to Korean companies depends on when China's capacity additions take full effect, with some pointing to 2028 as the turning point. If large volumes of new Chinese output arrive as AI investment growth slows, the article says, commodity memory prices could come under downward pressure.

Articles.Title: AI Memory Boom Is Funding China's Chip Catch-Up - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: YouTube Flags AI Music, Korean Platforms Lag Behind
stories.Summary:
YouTube has begun labeling songs made mainly with generative AI, letting users open the label for more detail, according to a report from Seoul Economic Daily published on October 22, 2026. The label went live on the 14th of that month, and the company identifies such content through partnerships with music industry players plus its own detection technology. It plans to extend the labels to the main YouTube app. Spotify has also been attaching an "AI persona" badge to profiles of virtual artists since last month, and Deezer said on the 13th that it would let users exclude fully AI-generated songs from search results within this year.

Major Korean services including Melon, Flo and Bugs have not introduced any separate labeling for AI-generated music, industry officials said on the same day. The companies cite the lack of clear criteria for judging how much AI was involved in a track, along with unclear rules for copyright recognition. Melon and its peers say they are discussing the issue internally and want to respond quickly once guidelines exist. Meanwhile, songs by so-called AI singers are already being distributed on Korean platforms.

The volume of AI-made music is climbing quickly. Deezer says the daily number of fully AI-generated songs arriving on its platform rose from 10,000 in January last year to 90,000 in June this year. In Korea, applications to register AI-generated music with the Korea Music Copyright Association rose from 133 last year to 759 through September this year, according to the office of Rep. Yoon Yong-keun of the People Power Party. The association withdrew a plan to allow trust registration of partly AI-made works after 22 days, and says it is developing identification technology, though details and timing have not been set.

Experts argue that clear criteria are needed so users can tell whether content was generated by AI. Kim Kyung-hwan, an attorney at law firm Minwho, said both legal and illegal content could emerge without such standards, and that order online depends on users being able to screen out AI-generated material. The association has said it will review supplementary measures reflecting discussions at the National Assembly and government as well as stakeholder opinions. The article does not say when Korean platforms will adopt labels or filters.

Articles.Title: YouTube Flags AI Music, Korean Platforms Lag Behind - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Seoul Forum Asks What Art and Humans Mean in the Age of AI
stories.Summary:
The Seoul Foundation for Arts and Culture said on October 22, 2026 that it will host the 2026 Seoul International Arts Forum, known as SAFT, on November 17 at Art Hall 2 of the Dongdaemun Design Plaza. The forum asks what role remains uniquely human and uniquely artistic as artificial intelligence takes on thinking and creating work. Now in its second year, it will bring together 12 experts from Korea and abroad in fields including AI, art, philosophy, literature and urban cultural policy. The theme is "Unfamiliar Intelligence and New Intellect: Designing the Age of Humans, Again." The organizers present it as a chance to revisit the meaning of art and of being human as technology reshapes daily life and social order.

The program has three sessions, one each on humans, art and the city. The first session will examine what human thought and judgment mean as machine intelligence advances, with speakers including Daniel Lee of Cornell University, Kim Sang-hyun of the Korea Institute for Advanced Study and artist Lawrence Lek. The second session will look at the value of art in an age of AI-assisted creation, drawing on human experience, sensation and imagination, with participants including science fiction writer Cheon Seon-ran, philosopher Nicolai Pedersen of Yonsei University and media artist Trevor Paglen. The final session will focus on how art connects people and builds community, with Łukasz Twarkowski, Glyn Roberts and Eva Soria Puig considering future cities through performance, festivals and urban cultural policy.

The agenda was shaped by talks with about 40 experts and by 53 topics proposed by citizens in six countries. The Seoul Foundation for Arts and Culture, whose chief executive is Song Hyung-jong, is the body behind the event. Media artist Lee Jin-joon, head of the Art & Technology Center at KAIST, will serve as overall host. Song said he hopes intellects from different fields will come together so that Seoul becomes a place that sends out future agendas and leads global discourse through art.

The article does not describe any formal policy change or binding outcome from the forum. The article places the forum within a broader public debate over what AI means for creative work and human judgment, though it does not describe specific follow-up steps beyond the November 17 event itself. Its reporting is based on the foundation's announcement and was translated from Korean with AI assistance, so foreign speakers' quotes may not match their original wording. The article does not say whether the forum will publish a report or continue in later years.

Articles.Title: Seoul Forum Asks What Art and Humans Mean in the Age of AI - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: KT Cloud Breaks Ground on 50MW AI Data Center in Ansan
stories.Summary:
KT Cloud broke ground on a 50-megawatt artificial intelligence data center in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province, and announced the project on October 22. The company said the facility is a company-owned building and is part of its long-term plan to secure 1 gigawatt of AI data center capacity by 2031. The aim is to expand AI data center capacity in the Seoul metropolitan area by securing the power and cooling needed for high-performance GPU servers. The facility is scheduled for completion in 2029.

The Ansan AI Data Center will cover a gross floor area of about 36,878 square meters, with two basement levels and nine floors above ground. Its total incoming power capacity will be 50 megawatts. All server rooms will be designed to support liquid cooling, and the building structure is intended to carry heavier equipment and higher server densities, including Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin GPUs. The project follows the opening of the Gasan AI Data Center in 2025 and adds capacity for high-heat AI servers. KT Cloud also plans a free-cooling system with cooling coils on the building's upper exterior walls, connected to closed-circuit cooling towers, which would use natural airflow in spring, autumn and winter to cut the electricity used by cooling tower fans and chillers.

KT Cloud is the party responsible for the project, and the company announced the groundbreaking itself. The articles provide no further statements from company officials beyond the stated goals of expanding capacity and improving cooling efficiency. The project fits within the company's broader strategy for AI infrastructure in the region. The articles do not say what other milestones or approvals may follow before the 2029 completion date.

Articles.Title: KT Cloud Breaks Ground on 50MW AI Data Center in Ansan - www.thelec.net

stories.Headline: Jay Y. Lee Visits UAE to Expand Samsung's Middle East AI Data Center Push
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Jay Y. Lee traveled to the United Arab Emirates, where he visited the construction site of the Al Dhafra gas-fired power plant in Abu Dhabi on November 21, local time, as the company reported on October 22. The trip was his first to the Middle East since he accompanied President Lee Jae-myung to the UAE last November. He toured major facilities at the plant, reviewed the construction schedule and safety management, and met with employees. At the site, he also held a meeting with executives from Samsung C&T and Samsung E&A on business strategy and new market entry.

Samsung said it is expanding its existing nuclear power and combined-cycle gas power businesses in line with the UAE's industrial development. The company is also looking for chances to join future projects in AI data centers and energy infrastructure. The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar are moving quickly to build data centers and power plants as AI adoption spreads across the region. Samsung Electronics, Samsung C&T and Samsung SDS plan to take part in designing, building and operating AI data centers. They also plan to supply advanced semiconductors and cooling equipment and to help construct power plants.

The company framed the visit as part of a push to move the group into new local businesses in a region the articles describe as still unsettled by war. Lee's presence at the site and his talks with the affiliate executives signal that the group is directing senior attention to the effort. The articles do not give investment amounts, contract values or timelines for any new AI data center or energy project. They also do not report any agreement signed during the visit. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Jay Y. Lee Visits UAE to Expand Samsung's Middle East AI Data Center Push - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Man Hires Swarm of AI Agents to Go on Epic Hacking Spree Against Major Companies
stories.Summary:
A Chinese-speaking hacker used swarms of autonomous AI agents to attack more than 100 companies, a case that a threat researcher at the cybersecurity firm NorForge uncovered and that Reuters first reported. The victims included John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, along with dozens of others. The researcher, Snorre Fagerland, said the hacker was one of several malicious actors who had abused an open source AI tool called Cairn to send agents out on autonomous hacking sprees. One of the Cairn-assisted hackers he observed was able to take sensitive credit card information. Fagerland described the shift bluntly, saying the world had changed.

The most aggressive operation, according to Reuters, deployed AI systems against more than 1,200 e-commerce sites in the United States, Canada, Australian and Japan. Successful breaches came after the agents had been attacking different companies for about 23 hours. Each successful hack reportedly cost about $50 in tokens. Fagerland said the techniques the agents used were sophisticated and not the work of inexperienced "script kiddies." The episode shows how a single person can now direct many always-on agents at once, multiplying the threat that one hacker can pose.

Deere told Reuters it had taken necessary remediation actions and saw no sign that sensitive information was accessed. SharkNinja said the hacker had reached a site that did not contain sensitive data. Cummins said it was investigating a potential cyberattack on a website run by one of its third-party vendors. The companies therefore offered different accounts of what was exposed, and the articles do not establish how much damage each breach caused. The report adds to a broader picture in which advanced AI can find and exploit existing weaknesses in widely used code.

Articles.Title: Man Hires Swarm of AI Agents to Go on Epic Hacking Spree Against Major Companies

stories.Headline: Samsung Chairman Visits UAE to Pitch AI Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Jay Y. Lee traveled to the United Arab Emirates, where he visited the Al Dhafra gas-fired power plant construction site on November 21, local time. The article, published October 22, 2026, describes the trip as his first to the Middle East in about a year. Lee chose the site, a $1.35 billion project won by Samsung C&T in a consortium with UAE builder Trojan General Contracting, which is scheduled to begin operating next year and will supply about one gigawatt of electricity to AI data centers. During his visit he also held an on-site strategy meeting and shared a meal with employees who stayed at the site despite the unstable situation.

The article says Samsung plans to move beyond supplying individual products and equipment and to target the UAE market with a combined offer spanning AI and energy infrastructure. It describes the opportunity as covering power generation and transmission, semiconductors, cooling equipment, data center operations and direct investment. Samsung Electronics is cited for advanced chips, its subsidiary FläktGroup for cooling, Samsung SDS for data center operations and Samsung SDI for energy storage systems. Samsung C&T's past work includes the Barakah nuclear plant and the Al Dhafra plant, and it signed a memorandum of understanding with Emirates Nuclear Energy Corp. in July of last year. Samsung E&A won the TAZIZ methanol project in the UAE last year.

The article attributes the strategy to the group's own conclusions and to industry watchers, and it quotes an unnamed business community official saying the scope for cooperation with Samsung affiliates is widening as the UAE moves toward advanced manufacturing. It also notes that Lee has built solid networks with senior UAE figures and discussed cooperation with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in November of last year. Against the backdrop of UAE plans to move away from an oil-centered economy, the article lists large projects, including roughly $150 billion in energy infrastructure by 2030 from Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. and the Stargate UAE AI computing cluster, whose first 200-megawatt facility is targeted to begin operating this year. It also reports that six Samsung companies invested $1 billion last month in Helix Digital Infrastructure, a firm set up by KKR. The article does not say what orders or investments, if any, will result from the visit.

Articles.Title: Samsung Chairman Visits UAE to Pitch AI Infrastructure - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Keeping a human in the AI loop is ‘untenable’ due to cuts, USDA IT official says
stories.Summary:
At a FedInsider Innovation Summit in Washington, D.C., on a Wednesday in October 2026, Rudolf Rojas, the USDA's IT program manager and security lead, said the department could no longer keep a human in the loop for artificial intelligence tasks. He called that approach "untenable" because cuts to government staffing and resources have left the agency without enough people or contract support. Rojas said USDA will need to get smarter and use AI tools to do the work and then report back to staff. He framed the shift as a practical necessity rather than a choice the agency wants to make.

Rojas said agents would not be allowed to run unchecked, and he wants them to have minimal privileges and a minimal role. He would let agents operate without a person only if an agency has a strong risk management framework, has analyzed its networks, and has a well-defined demilitarized zone, as USDA does. Using zero-trust principles, he said, lets the agency continuously monitor its networks and tools. He also said vendors will have to improve how they build AI into the products the government buys. Taken together, he described the approach as a balance that still needs out-of-the-box thinking.

Rojas said he believes the nation needs to coalesce around rules and regulations for AI, and he said he somewhat disagrees with the administration's stated position that AI companies should have free rein. He pointed to past regulation of railroads and nuclear energy as examples of workable oversight. He argued that rules are needed so the government can use these tools safely and guard against bad actors, which he linked to China, Russia, and other nation-state adversaries. Ajay Phogat, senior advisor to the chief information officer at U.S. Customs and Border Protection, took a different view. He said he favors humans in the loop and called the threat AI poses to security real as things stand today.

Other agency officials at the summit described their own AI efforts as growing and accelerating alongside governance. The National Institutes of Health is building an AI deployment infrastructure to set policies for data, finance, and governance, and the Library of Congress is running AI sandbox experiments that have drawn more proposals than it can support. The State Department is building AI training into new foreign service officer instruction and says its StateChat chatbot saves people about two hours a week on average. Kevin Walsh, director of the IT and cybersecurity team at the Government Accountability Office, warned that the government is over its skis and lacks enough oversight to fully understand the technology. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Keeping a human in the AI loop is ‘untenable’ due to cuts, USDA IT official says

stories.Headline: What’s New in Digital Equity: New York’s AI Jobs Institute
stories.Summary:
Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York announced the AI Jobs Institute, a Queens-based hub designed to connect New Yorkers to careers in artificial intelligence. The institute will offer AI upskilling to help residents reach technology-related career pathways. It will also incubate pilots and tools, produce data and recommendations for state and federal AI workforce strategies, and build a collaborative network among employers, talent and industry partners. The state expects it to train up to 40,000 New Yorkers by 2032.

The institute will be powered by Pursuit, a nonprofit tech workforce training and job placement organization that pairs training with long-term employer partnerships. Empire State Development is providing $3.06 million, made up of $1.5 million from the Office of Strategic Workforce Development and $1.56 million from the Regional Economic Development Council initiative. Backing also comes from Queens Borough President Donovan Richards, city partners and a coalition of philanthropic, industry and civic groups, including Wells Fargo, Anthropic and the Partnership Fund for New York City. A National Advisory Council will guide the work, with founding members including Félix V. Matos Rodríguez, chancellor of the City University of New York, former U.S. Education Secretary Miguel Cardona and Julie Samuels, CEO of Tech:NYC.

Officials said the institute will also house the New York Global Tech and Innovation Center, which aims to connect underrepresented entrepreneurs with capital, partnerships and networks. Its stated goal is to create more than a dozen high-growth startups over the next five years. Officials framed the effort as a way to keep New York competitive by preparing its people for an economy that technology is reshaping. The announcement says the institute will support state and federal AI workforce planning through the data it produces. The article notes that experts expect AI to create the next digital divide, which is why some digital inclusion practitioners are adding AI skills to their training.

Articles.Title: What’s New in Digital Equity: New York’s AI Jobs Institute

stories.Headline: AI stocks tumble as the defensives rise. What it says about this uneasy market
stories.Summary:
Stocks fell on Thursday, October 22, 2026, as another wave of selling hit the artificial intelligence trade. The article says Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC there is a scarcity of capital for neoclouds such as CoreWeave, even though compute demand is very strong. Chipmaking equipment provider Lam Research gave weak guidance for the current quarter, which also weighed on semiconductor names such as Micron and Intel. GE Vernova, whose gas turbines are part of the AI buildout, was down almost 10 percent, a sharp reversal from the day before. The report comes from CNBC's Investing Club recap of the session.

Money moved into defensive sectors as the AI names slid. Healthcare and consumer staples were the best-performing sectors in the S&P 500 even though oil prices rose on Thursday. Bond yields moved lower, which the article describes as a flight-to-safety trade. Johnson & Johnson gained more than 2 percent, erasing its post-earnings sell-off, and Kimberly-Clark was back near the level where the Club initiated its position on September 2. The article notes that Procter & Gamble reported a solid quarter that day but did not change the Club's preference for Kimberly-Clark.

Meta Platforms fell nearly 6 percent despite strong revenue growth reported Wednesday night and an upbeat outlook for its Muse AI agent business. The article points to Meta's plan to create a new class of non-voting stock, which is likely to help fund its AI buildout, as a possible overhang. Portfolio director Jeff Marks said the stock had given back most of its post-Muse gains, which began when Muse launched on September 8. The Club sold 35 shares on September 22 after a parabolic move, and Marks said it would stay patient rather than buy back in yet. He added that recent purchases have been outside the tech group.

The article frames these moves as a rotation out of tech and into defensive pockets, with Marks observing that the market has no memory from one day to the next. It does not describe any further action beyond the Club's stated patience with Meta and its continued interest in the Kenvue acquisition pending at Kimberly-Clark. The piece is a daily recap, so it does not give a forecast for how long the rotation will last. Jim Cramer's charitable trust holds several of the stocks discussed, including Meta, Micron, Intel, Lam Research, GE Vernova, Johnson & Johnson, Kimberly-Clark and Nvidia.

Articles.Title: AI stocks tumble as the defensives rise. What it says about this uneasy market

stories.Headline: The AI Race Is Getting Weird—and May Never End
stories.Summary:
This is not a news event with a breaking development but an excerpt from a book promotion: Kevin Roose, a technology journalist and co-host of the podcast Machine Gods, shares five insights from his new book, The AGI Chronicles, published on the Next Big Idea Club site on October 22, 2026. The piece argues that the race to build artificial general intelligence is strange and may never reach a clear finish line, because the goalposts keep moving as systems become more capable. Roose's central claim is that we are already living in the early, imperfect years of AGI and that institutions are dangerously unprepared for what follows. Roose describes a founding paradox in which many of the researchers building AI got into the field because they feared it. He sorts the field into three groups: scientists who want to cure disease, seekers who see AI as an evolutionary turning point, and survivalists who believe the technology must be built by the right people before someone worse builds it.

According to the excerpt, Dario Amodei left OpenAI partly out of concern it was moving too fast, then founded Anthropic, a competitor that also had to accelerate to stay ahead. Roose also recounts that the breakthrough came from a simple recipe, which Amodei outlined in a 2017 paper called "Big Blob of Compute," in which a neural network is fed huge amounts of data and given a large amount of computing power. Roose writes that insiders have a shared sense of purpose he calls "feeling the AGI," which he attributes to former OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever. The excerpt says that for years everyone in the race assumed it would end once someone built a system as smart as the smartest humans, and that leaders even planned their retirements around that moment. Roose says the picture changed around 2025, when the competition came to resemble an endless race in which rivals match each other's breakthroughs and nobody agrees on what AGI means or how to recognize it.

He ties this to the Red Queen's race from Lewis Carroll and says the field keeps running without getting anywhere relative to competitors. In the final section, Roose argues that by the 2016 definition of a machine doing most cognitive tasks about as well as most humans, the goal has already been reached. He says today's models can write, code, analyze documents, and pass professional exams, though their abilities are uneven, which is why many people still doubt that AGI has arrived. His larger warning is that the greater risk lies in society's institutions, including governments, companies, schools, and communities, continuing to act as though the technology has not already changed. The excerpt closes by urging the public to catch up with researchers who have been feeling the AGI for years.

Articles.Title: The AI Race Is Getting Weird—and May Never End

stories.Headline: Professor Kim Jung-ho: "South Korea's Chip Success Wasn't Just Technology—It Was a Windfall… HBM Was Decisive"
stories.Summary:
Professor Kim Jung-ho of Yonsei University has argued that South Korea's semiconductor success came from unexpected external factors as much as from technical skill. In a recent appearance on a YouTube channel, he said the flagship businesses of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix benefited from the AI boom in ways their original plans had not anticipated. He noted that Samsung aimed to lead in system semiconductors and saw its market share decline, while DRAM, its traditional mainstay, unexpectedly boomed as AI grew. He described the result as less a feat South Korea pulled off than a windfall that arrived on its own.

SK Hynix's investment in high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, was another example he gave. HBM stacks multiple DRAM chips vertically to raise data processing speed and efficiency, which makes it important for AI chips that need heavy computation. Kim said SK Hynix kept developing HBM even while the company was under financial strain. HBM initially gained little traction in the gaming PC market, but demand changed once ChatGPT drove rapid growth in AI, since data centers needed high-performance GPUs and memory that could keep pace with them. Kim summed up the value of HBM by saying it resolves the bottleneck in which GPUs run fast but memory cannot keep up.

Kim also pointed to possible openings for South Korea's battery industry. Chinese companies dominate electric vehicle batteries through mass production and price competitiveness, but he argued a different landscape could emerge in physical AI fields such as robotics. Because human-sized robots have limited room for batteries, high energy density matters, and he said South Korean batteries hold an advantage there. He also highlighted solid-state batteries, which address limits of conventional liquid-electrolyte designs, and said South Korea and Japan are strong contenders in commercializing them. He named defense combined with AI and drones as the next industry to develop, and stressed the need to reform education so that people can master AI.

Ahead of these discussions, the Smart Energy Plus (SEP) 2026 conference is scheduled for the 29th at COEX in Gangnam District, Seoul, where senior executives from both companies will speak about the future of AI and semiconductors. Han Jae-jun, a master, or managing director, at Samsung Electronics' AX/PI Center, will present a strategy for integrating AI from design through production, and Samsung will disclose a case in which automated techniques cut design time by about 50%. Choi Jun-yong, vice president of HBM business planning at SK Hynix, will discuss how the performance bottleneck has moved from computing to memory and now to power. He will address the "Energy Wall" created by rising data center power use and propose solutions such as higher bandwidth per watt and 3D stacking. Kim's analysis suggests that investment decisions should weigh how unpredictable AI demand is reshaping memory markets, not just the planned success of any one technology.

Articles.Title: Professor Kim Jung-ho: "South Korea's Chip Success Wasn't Just Technology—It Was a Windfall… HBM Was Decisive" - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: From Eyeballs to ARR: Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the AI Trade!
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company, held a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors on October 15, 2026, in San Francisco, where it reported third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, up 45% over the prior quarter, along with positive profits on an adjusted basis. The company also reported an annual revenue run rate of $67 billion and an estimate that this figure could exceed $100 billion by year end. The articles note that these figures are tied to a foundation for an upcoming public offering, and that run-rate calculations depend on choices about gross versus net revenue and annualization periods. Analyst Aswath Damodaran, writing on October 22, 2026, said he was not present at the meeting but shared some skepticism about comparing these numbers across time and companies.

He argued that young businesses are commonly priced on unconventional metrics, pointing to dot-com era eyeballs and social media user counts as earlier examples. Damodaran explains that companies can be classified as young or mature by chronological age, by industry grouping, or by operating metrics such as revenue growth, operating losses, negative free cash flow and failure risk. Under those tests, he says, a firm with high growth, thin or negative margins and large negative free cash flow is a young growth company regardless of its size. He applies this to Anthropic and OpenAI, noting their rapid growth and operating losses while observing that both already have large revenues on a run-rate basis.

He says both companies' business models remain in flux and that Anthropic's claimed second-quarter 2026 profitability relies on adjustments he doubts. He also reports that both firms are deep in negative free cash flow, and that their future depends on how the AI business develops. Damodaran contrasts intrinsic valuation, which estimates value from expected cash flows, growth and risk, with pricing, which reflects what others pay for similar assets. He says valuing young companies is harder because financial statements are noisy and history is short, and he argues that many investors will therefore rely on pricing signals.

He points to venture capital rounds as one such signal. Anthropic raised $65 billion in May 2026 at a post-money valuation of $965 billion, while OpenAI raised $122 billion in March 2026 at $852 billion. OpenAI also has a pending round expected to raise $30 billion at roughly $1.4 trillion ahead of an IPO. Damodaran cautions that venture capital pricing is itself part of the pricing game and should not be assumed to reflect intrinsic value.

Articles.Title: From Eyeballs to ARR: Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the AI Trade!

stories.Headline: CSUF: California economy pumped up by AI, but weak hiring persists
stories.Summary:
California's economy grew faster than the nation's in the first half of 2026, according to economists at California State University, Fullerton, who presented their annual forecast in Irvine on Thursday, October 22, 2026. The growth was driven by large investments in artificial intelligence and defense spending, even as hiring stayed weak and consumer confidence slid. Anil Puri and Mira Farka, who direct the Woods Center for Economic Analysis and Forecasting, said the state's gross domestic product rose 3.5% compared with the same period a year earlier, versus 2.4% nationally. Their 94-page report focused largely on how AI is reshaping the economy.

The economists said AI now accounts for 37% of California's growth, nearly double its share in 2023 and 2024 and well above the 27% share nationally. They warned that the Southern California jobs market could suffer if it becomes too concentrated in AI, especially if the boom turns into a bubble. Farka said at least 17% of Orange County's workforce faces disruption from AI, which she expects to shift jobs rather than simply replace them. Puri said the most exposed local sectors include professional services, information technology, and finance and insurance. Both suggested workforce training could help workers adapt to those changes.

Farka said the national economy is in balance with AI and jobs, but the local economy is not. The economists do not expect a recession, though they see growth slowing, with national GDP rising 2.2% in the second quarter after 2.5% in the first. They also expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again this year, followed by increases in 2027, to combat inflation driven by an oil price shock linked to the U.S.-led war in Iran. The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, and the Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point that month, its first increase in more than three years. Puri and Farka expect one more hike this year and two in 2027.

The economists described a labor market they called the "Great Stasis," a period of few hires, few firings and few people quitting that has lasted nearly two years. Job growth across Orange County, Los Angeles County and the Inland Empire has slowed to a small fraction of its pre-pandemic pace. Housing is also stalled, with the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate reaching 7.4% earlier in October, its highest in nearly three years, before easing to 7.32%. Savings have fallen to 4.1% of disposable income, and credit card balances climbed to $1.26 trillion. Still, the report noted that the aerospace and defense sector is growing, with Orange County employment in that sector up 8.4% in 2025 to about 22,600 jobs.

Articles.Title: CSUF: California economy pumped up by AI, but weak hiring persists

stories.Headline: Gene editing scientists slowed down for safety. Could AI leaders follow their guide?
stories.Summary:
In 1971, Janet Mertz, a biochemistry graduate student, planned an experiment combining a cancer-causing virus with E. coli, and biologist Bob Pollack warned that the work could be dangerous and could even spread cancer. Her thesis adviser canceled the experiment, and the concern spread through the field as researchers realized that the new technique of cutting DNA from one organism and pasting it into another could carry serious risks. The technology was also seen as promising, with possibilities such as mass-produced insulin, self-fertilizing plants and cures for diseases. Because no single lab wanted to fall behind or give rivals the lead, the field faced a collective action problem.

In 1974, Mertz's boss and other lab heads published an open letter calling for a pause in their cutting-edge research so they could meet and agree on new safety measures. That meeting became known as the Asilomar conference, where leading scientists debated what guardrails to adopt or whether to impose any at all. Bioethicist Alex Capron, one of the few nonscientists present, argued that freedom of thought did not extend to freedom to cause physical injury to others. He warned that if the researchers did not regulate themselves, Congress might step in. In the end, most participants agreed on laboratory protocols and other safeguards.

The story is presented as a precedent for the artificial intelligence industry, where some leaders of the AI race are now calling for a slowdown for safety reasons. The report frames that call as a collective action problem, since no company wants to slow down unless its rivals do too. The episode is described in a segment of NPR's Planet Money, and its host and reporter draw the parallel directly, asking whether AI industry leaders could follow the same path. The articles do not describe any specific AI agreement, pause or regulatory measure being adopted at this time.

Articles.Title: Gene editing scientists slowed down for safety. Could AI leaders follow their guide?

stories.Headline: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, October 22, 2026, password manager 1Password launched a new tool called 1Password for Agents, which lets users allow AI agents to log into their personal accounts without the agent ever seeing their credentials. When an agent tries to log in, 1Password receives a unique digital key to confirm the agent's identity, and the user receives an alert about the attempt and can personally approve it. Once approved, 1Password signs the agent in by filling in the credentials on its behalf, so the agent can complete the task. Users can choose among several agents, including Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI's Dots and ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta's Muse, and agents from the startup Town, and the company says it is working with other firms to expand the service.

The company argues that handing over a password is a common shortcut that can leave sensitive information in places a person can no longer control, since a copy may be saved for future use. In its blog post, 1Password said the platform gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks need. The launch came the same day Axios reported that U.S. banks have started detecting agentic activity inside user accounts. The article notes this is not necessarily rogue agents taking over accounts, but rather consumers increasingly letting automated services act for them, including on financial matters.

The main concern raised is that most banks cannot tell whether that agentic activity reflects a user's actual request. Bankers interviewed by Axios described the situation as horrifying, and a Chase spokesperson told the outlet that customers should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone. The article is written by TechCrunch senior writer Lucas, who covers artificial intelligence and consumer tech. The coverage places the launch in a broader effort by security services to catch up with the access consumers are entrusting to AI agents, and the articles do not say what banks plan to do in response.

Articles.Title: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password

stories.Headline: Retail Traders Loaded Up on AI Spending Winners Before Selloff
stories.Summary:
Retail investors spent the past week buying semiconductor stocks at the heart of the artificial intelligence trade, then took heavy losses when chipmakers fell sharply on Thursday. According to JPMorgan Chase & Co. strategist Arun Jain, who looked at trading flows from last Thursday through Wednesday, individual investors increased purchases of chipmakers, neocloud service providers and memory device makers while buying of the Magnificent Seven technology stocks weakened. Single-stock technology buying reached its highest level since the momentum unwind began in July, he wrote in a note to clients on Wednesday. The selloff hit on Thursday as worries about the Mideast conflict and extravagant AI infrastructure spending weighed on chipmakers, and a gauge of semiconductor stocks fell 6.7%, its worst day since June.

The stocks retail traders bought most were SanDisk Corp., Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and Nebius Group NV, and each dropped at least 4% on Thursday. SpaceX shares ranked fourth on that list through Tuesday, but investors sold them on Wednesday after they jumped 7.8% on the company's encouraging earnings report. Retail demand was even stronger for technology exchange-traded funds, where weekly inflows reached their second-highest level on record. Friday brought the largest single-day inflow into tech ETFs on record, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF was among the funds drawing heavy interest. Market strategists describe this shift as a move toward broader exposure rather than an exit from the AI theme.

Joe Gilbert, a portfolio manager at Integrity Asset Management, said investors have rotated from the Magnificent Seven to technology more broadly because the AI ecosystem has produced more durable earnings than first expected. He added that robust earnings growth is possible at cheaper valuations, particularly with higher interest rates outside the Magnificent Seven group. The Bank of America Corp. data cited in the reporting show S&P 500 Information Technology companies are expected to post 66% earnings growth for the third quarter, trailing only energy and communication services. The sector's strong profit growth has kept investor interest alive even as fears of an AI bubble grow.

The selloff has also been fed by renewed concern about higher inflation from a spike in energy prices tied to the ongoing war in Iran. The Bloomberg Magnificent Seven Index fell as much as 3.8% on Thursday after Meta Platforms Inc. raised its capital spending plans for the year, while the Nasdaq 100 Index slid as much as 3.2%. Despite the enthusiasm for tech stocks, overall retail flows stayed subdued for the week, according to JPMorgan's data. The reporting does not say how the week's losses will affect retail positioning going forward.

Articles.Title: Retail Traders Loaded Up on AI Spending Winners Before Selloff

stories.Headline: App's AI 'eyes' for blind users fall short, researchers find
stories.Summary:
A University of Maryland study presented this year at the ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems found that an AI photo-description app often gave answers blind users did not want. The researchers tested the app Be My AI, part of Be My Eyes, with 11 participants who identify as blind. Participants used the app in a lab and then in daily life for 10 days before discussing their experiences with the team. The study examined 418 conversational interactions and recorded in its findings the results described below.

The team found that users typically asked questions of 10 to 20 words, while the app's responses used more than 10 times as many words. Some conversations stretched to 21 back-and-forth exchanges, which can be frustrating because blind users hear every answer read aloud. The app also opens each conversation with a full description of the photo, even when the user only had a question about one part of it. More than half the participants called this a serious problem, and one user said she only wanted to find her keys. The researchers said that delays in time-sensitive situations can create safety concerns.

The study's authors are Farnaz Zamiri Zeraati, Hernisa Kacorri, Hal Daumé III, Yuehan Qiao and Yang Trista Cao, with Kacorri, an associate professor in the College of Information, and Daumé, a computer science professor and director of the NSF Institute for Trustworthy AI in Law and Society, among those named. Kacorri said that these systems are getting better at generating descriptions but often fail to capture user intent, which turns into lengthy responses rather than useful answers. Qiao said blind users still do much of the work of figuring out which information is relevant. The researchers argued that users should not need special skills to get usable answers, calling a complex prompting strategy a workaround for a limitation of the technology.

To cope, participants borrowed techniques from general-purpose AI tools and invented their own. Some explained why they were asking a question, and one photographed her kitchen and stated her goal of remodeling it. Others split big tasks into small questions, such as asking about the size, surface, bubbles and flour of bread dough one at a time. The researchers believe this is the first study to systematically document how such strategies work for blind people in assistive settings. The paper appeared in the 2026 CHI Conference proceedings.

Articles.Title: App's AI 'eyes' for blind users fall short, researchers find

stories.Headline: AI debt and French bonds face a stress test — why it may not be over
stories.Summary:
Credit markets are sending warning signals about debt tied to the AI infrastructure boom and about France's public finances, according to a CNBC analysis published on October 22, 2026. Five-year credit default swap spreads have widened for CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank Group, as well as for France and Italy. The article says AI-related bonds have been selling off as markets raise the cost of capital amid concerns about a financing crunch. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC that demand is "off the charts" but warned of a scarcity of capital. Recent mass protests and rioting in France have also heightened investor concerns about the country's debt.

The spreads measure the cost of insuring against default, so higher readings mean investors want more compensation for the risk. CoreWeave's five-year spread reached 1,065.84 basis points on October 21, according to FactSet, reflecting worry about its ability to finance expansion. Oracle's spread rose to 308.25 basis points on October 21, up from 141 on January 2, after S&P Credit Ratings cut its debt to the lowest level of investment grade in July. SoftBank's spread stood near a four-year high of 432 basis points on October 20, up from 284 on January 5, and the company has an $87 billion commitment for data centers in France. France's five-year spread reached 89.8 basis points on October 21, up from 29.74 on January 2, now above Italy's 67.1 basis points.

Macquarie strategist Thierry Wizman pointed to France's sovereign debt, which he put at 120% of GDP, and its inability to reduce the deficit as the main drivers, compared with German government debt at 65% of GDP. Ben Emons, chief investment officer of FedWatch Advisors, wrote that markets may no longer want to finance heavy leverage and uncertain future cash flows, which is also widening French spreads. The article attributes these views to the analysts themselves and does not describe any formal action by the companies or the French government. France is not in a full-fledged debt crisis, the article notes, though its 10-year bond yield topped 5% for the first time since 2002. The gap between French and German 10-year bonds has surged to 1.6 percentage points, still well below the spreads seen during the early 2010s eurozone debt crisis.

Broader pressure is also visible across the market. S&P Global warned on October 19 that major cloud providers may have more AI-linked debt exposure than is publicly recognized. North America's CDX High Yield index reached a five-year midpoint spread of 355.35 basis points on October 20, up about 39 basis points from the end of 2025, according to LSEG data. The article reports that this widening suggests investors are demanding more compensation for credit risk beyond AI-linked borrowers. The next test for France comes on October 23, when Moody's is scheduled to review its Aa3 sovereign rating, which carries a negative outlook, amid political divisions over repairing the public finances.

Articles.Title: AI debt and French bonds face a stress test — why it may not be over

stories.Headline: AI products fuel spending during National Day holiday
stories.Summary:
During the weeklong National Day holiday in early October, shoppers across China crowded into stores to try the latest artificial intelligence gadgets, as smart devices continue moving from showrooms into the mass market. At Z. Pilot, an AI experience store in Shanghai, a furry AI pet robot drew a steady stream of browsers, with its digital eyes lighting up in a feeding expression when offered a toy carrot. Employees said companionship products were selling well, since the pets offer voice and touch interaction and gradually adapt to their owners over time. AI glasses, which handle real-time translation, navigation, teleprompting and photo and video capture, also drew strong interest in the city.

Demand reached beyond Shanghai. At a JD.com mall in the Qibao area, families gathered around 3D printers, and parents said they bought them so children could design and print their own models at home. In Hangzhou, a tech mall called Wensan brought together more than 700 smart products, from AI companion robots and AI glasses to smart rings and exoskeletons, for consumers of all ages. In Beijing, a robotics and AI experience brand under Shoucheng Holdings operates eight stores offering more than 200 robot and AI hardware products, and it drew long queues during the holiday, with particularly strong results for companion-style AI, entertainment devices and interactive robotics. Retailers are also reporting measurable gains: according to Suning.com, foot traffic at its flagship stores rose 50 percent year on year from October 1 to 7, while sales of AI-equipped home appliances climbed more than 40 percent, and smartwatches, AI glasses and action cameras all posted solid increases.

The article ties this consumer surge to a wider AI expansion in China. It reports that AI enterprises in the country passed 6,000 last year and that China had more than 140 humanoid robot developers in 2025, with shipments reaching 14,400 units, or 84.7 percent of the global market, according to an industry research report. Government policy has also pushed the trend forward: in June, eight departments, including the Ministry of Commerce, issued guidance to boost AI-enabled consumption, and a later action plan on smart home consumption let localities set their own subsidy categories and standards under the 2026 trade-in policy, including support for whole-house smart home purchases. Fan Chunyan, vice-president of Suning.com, said consumer uptake of AI products is moving from novelty toward mass adoption and that demand for smart devices, immersive experiences and ongoing services will keep rising.

Articles.Title: AI products fuel spending during National Day holiday - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Nasdaq & Chip Stocks Plunge: Jensen Huang’s Stock Touting Fails as Market Delivers Heavy Blow to AI Bulls
stories.Summary:
On October 22, Thursday, U.S. chip and tech stocks sold off sharply, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 2.6% in its largest single-day drop since June and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sliding about 6.72%. Shares of NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Micron and TSMC all slumped, and Meta's stock fell nearly 7%. The move followed Meta's quarterly report, in which heavier capital spending pushed its free cash flow negative to 2.12 billion U.S. dollars. Oil prices rose on Middle East tensions, adding to worries about inflation and interest rates.

The selloff did not come out of nowhere. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had already fallen for eight straight trading days through October 16, losing more than 15% in total. Data from Goldman Sachs' prime brokerage showed hedge funds cutting tech holdings at the fastest pace in at least ten years in the five sessions ending October 15, with semiconductors among the biggest reductions. Retail investors, by contrast, were buying chip, storage and AI cloud stocks on the dip, according to JPMorgan strategist Arun Jain's flow data for October 15 to 21.

Several prominent market figures voiced concern about the spending. Citadel founder Ken Griffin told foreign media on October 20 that investors are almost certain there is an AI bubble, comparing GPUs to airlines with very low marginal costs that could see prices fall if supply outpaces demand. He also noted that businesses are scrutinizing AI bills from firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI and want clear productivity gains, while still arguing that the leading companies will matter for decades. Michael Burry, who gained fame for betting against the housing market, has reportedly moved most of his short exposure into Nasdaq 100 and semiconductor ETF puts, and he believes a major market top could arrive within nine months.

Leverage amplified the pain. CoinGlass data cited by CoinDesk showed about 51.6 million U.S. dollars of chip-linked crypto perpetual contracts were liquidated within 10 minutes during the U.S. stock holiday on October 17, with about 38 million dollars from long positions. Short sellers of new AI cloud and data center companies, including CoreWeave and Nebius, have earned large paper profits this month, according to ORTEX, with roughly 6 billion dollars in total gains. Yet the broader market was not uniformly weak, since nearly two-thirds of S&P 500 stocks closed higher on October 22 even as the index fell 1.21%.

Articles.Title: Nasdaq & Chip Stocks Plunge: Jensen Huang’s Stock Touting Fails as Market Delivers Heavy Blow to AI Bulls - 36Kr

stories.Headline: ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on AI: ‘An Amazing Piece of Technology’ But ‘I’m Not Embracing It at All’
stories.Summary:
Director Travis Knight, speaking at the AFI Fest opening night U.S. premiere of "Wildwood" on Wednesday night, said he is not embracing artificial intelligence. He described AI as an amazing piece of technology but said he sees it as a tool that is useful only when placed in the hands of artists. Knight drew a comparison to a pencil, a paintbrush and a 3D printer, all of which he called technology. The remarks came as he weighed in on Hollywood's use of AI. Knight's concern centers on generative AI taking the place of the artist rather than assisting one.

He said a computer cannot speak about humanity and does not know what it feels like. He argued that stop-motion animation represents human creativity, emotion, care, devotion and time, qualities he believes no machine can replicate. Asked whether AI could have sped up the production of "Wildwood," he said the very notion filled him with rage if the goal was to maintain the highest quality. He added that technology seems to be pushing everything toward being simpler, more automated and easier.

"Wildwood" is a stop-motion fantasy feature about a young girl, played by Peyton Elizabeth Lee, who travels into a forbidden forest after her baby brother is kidnapped by a murder of crows. Knight said the film took 16 years to complete and that it has been old enough to drive him to the premiere. He said the story is a big, sweeping adventure, but that an epic alone cannot sustain a project for that long. He said the heart of the film is something heartfelt and emotional, and that this is what he hopes audiences take away from it.

The voice cast includes Jacob Tremblay, Angela Bassett, Jake Johnson, Carey Mulligan, Maya Erskine, Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Amandla Stenberg and Tantoo Cardinal. Bassett, who recorded her role during COVID, said she wanted to get out of the house and be creative again, and that the project arrived right on time for her. The article's coverage of the premiere includes photos of the cast and guests at the event and after party. The article does not report any policy change, industry action or next steps tied to Knight's comments on AI.

Articles.Title: ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on AI: ‘An Amazing Piece of Technology’ But ‘I’m Not Embracing It at All’

stories.Headline: Natrona County and Prometheus Hyperscale consider bypassing state review for new AI complex
stories.Summary:
Natrona County officials in Wyoming are drafting a list of conditions, permits and expectations they would require of Prometheus Hyperscale, a company proposing a 1,250-megawatt artificial intelligence computing complex east of Casper. Commissioners told WyoFile that the main concerns are assurances that the data center's water use and electricity needs will not harm residents, along with measures to limit noise and light pollution and an assessment of whether the project would be a net benefit to the community. Commission Chairman Jim Milne said the process is only just beginning and could take a long time, with room to adjust terms along the way. The company first publicly floated the project last spring and presented it to commissioners at a packed meeting in September, when founder Trenton Thornock described himself as a sixth-generation Uinta County rancher.

The proposed facility would begin with an initial investment of about $500 million and has room to expand. Its designers say it would use a closed-loop cooling system to limit water use and injection wells to store carbon dioxide from a fleet of natural gas-fueled generators that would power the site apart from the public grid. Thornock also proposed bypassing the state's Industrial Siting Council process, a one-stop permitting review, and instead working directly with the county, which he argued would still meet all environmental and regulatory requirements. Typically, projects of this scale must undergo a Wyoming Industrial Siting Act review involving some 19 state and federal agencies. A so-called industrial park exemption allows developers to take this route when a county has strong zoning and development staff to handle the review.

Commissioner Dave North said the project would still have to satisfy state wildlife, water and other statutes, and that the change simply speeds the process up. He said the county could set its own specific requirements under this approach, and that a county lacking zoning and planning capacity would struggle with it. Milne and other commissioners have said the idea has appeal. Prometheus is already several phases into a similar process in Uinta County, where it is building another data center complex. The articles do not say when the commission will vote on a decision about the exemption or the final list of conditions.

Articles.Title: Natrona County and Prometheus Hyperscale consider bypassing state review for new AI complex

stories.Headline: Major Tech Giants' AI Products Face Accelerated Market Reshuffling: One Product Exits in Just 188 Days
stories.Summary:
Tencent said on September 24 that its QClaw AI product, part of a wave of personal agent tools, will shut down on December 24, 2026. Users will be given tools to move their data to another Tencent product, WorkBuddy. QClaw had entered public beta on March 20, so it lasted just 188 days before the shutdown was announced. The exit is one sign of a faster reshuffling across the AI product market. Eight companies, including Tencent, Alibaba, Baidu, ByteDance, Moonshot AI, Zhipu AI, MiniMax and DeepSeek, were tracked across ten AI business areas, from image generation to personal agents.

On October 13, Alibaba said it would soon release a personal assistant called Qwen Go!, which is meant to handle tasks such as flight delay claims, price comparisons and phone reservations. The article notes that products are being renamed, merged or shut down more often, and that many standalone tools are folding into broader general assistants. The article describes how the cycle has shortened over four years. Text-to-image tools drew attention in 2022, chatbots spread in 2023, and video generation and AI hardware followed in 2024. In March 2026 alone, five companies, including ByteDance, Tencent, Zhipu AI, Baidu and Alibaba, launched their own "Claw-like" products.

Alibaba and ByteDance cover all ten tracks, while DeepSeek covers only two. Companies are weighing which products deserve continued investment and which should be merged or ended, according to the article. Several examples are given: Baidu's Ernie Bot was renamed twice, Alibaba's Wukong was merged into Qwen Office in July 2026, and ByteDance's MarsCode became a TRAE plugin. The article also says general assistants are taking on more functions, such as search, file reading, drawing, research and code execution. Companies gain from consolidating development work, while users must relearn entry points each time a product is renamed or moved.

Articles.Title: Major Tech Giants' AI Products Face Accelerated Market Reshuffling: One Product Exits in Just 188 Days - 36Kr

stories.Headline: AMD Helion Puts CPU Density at the Center of Agentic AI Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
AMD unveiled Helion on October 12, 2026, at the Open Compute Project Global Summit in San Jose, California, as an open, modular rack-scale architecture for agentic AI. The design responds to a shift in workloads, where agents need substantial general-purpose computing alongside the GPU capacity used for model inference. Helion is built on OCP specifications and comes in two principal configurations. One is a CPU-only rack supporting up to 32,768 sixth-generation EPYC cores for large-scale agent execution, and the other pairs EPYC processors with Instinct MI350P accelerators for enterprise agent processing and inference. AMD says initial availability is targeted for November 2026, with commercial implementations to be built by industry partners.

The architecture lets operators scale CPU-based agent execution and GPU inference independently, which the company argues could improve utilization as the mix of demands changes. The enterprise configuration can hold up to 16 MI350P accelerators in two independent eight-GPU servers, each occupying five rack units, and it supports both air-cooled and liquid-cooled builds. AMD outlines three CPU options: high-density 256-core processors rated at 400 watts, balanced 256-core processors rated at 600 watts, and a high-frequency 96-core option running up to 5 GHz. The rack uses a 21-inch, 44 OpenU design based on the OCP Open Rack Version 3 specification. Helion also includes an integrated token-routing capability that directs requests between locally hosted open-source models and larger frontier models in external infrastructure.

AMD's Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager of Compute and Enterprise AI, said agentic AI spans personal agents, enterprise applications, code execution and complex workflows, each with different compute needs. He said AMD intends to combine EPYC performance, open software and flexible rack designs so partners can build systems around customer needs and use available power efficiently. Lisa Su, AMD's chief executive, said during her October 12 keynote that the company now projects the server CPU market will exceed $200 billion by 2030, up from an earlier estimate of $120 billion. The article presents that figure as AMD's own forecast rather than an independent measure of demand.

The context is that agentic AI could make general-purpose computing a larger share of data center load, which affects power, cooling, networking and the amount of useful capacity a facility can deliver. The article notes that AMD has not yet published full rack-level power and cooling requirements for the Helion configurations, and no independent workload benchmarks have been released. Without those figures, the claimed infrastructure efficiencies remain a design proposition rather than a demonstrated advantage. The article indicates that the outcome will depend on how partners implement the designs starting with the planned November 2026 availability.

Articles.Title: AMD Helion Puts CPU Density at the Center of Agentic AI Infrastructure

stories.Headline: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans
stories.Summary:
Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans: people are loyal to their group rather than to the truth. ModelCompare asked twelve text models from ten labs, in three countries, for their most controversial take on humans, three times each with no hedging. Every model gave the shared take at least once, and seven of the twelve gave it in all three answers. The test ran on October 22, 2026, and the results were published that day.

The shared take holds that people choose what their group believes and then invent reasons to defend it. Answers in this group said humans put belonging, status or their own story ahead of truth or principle, often calling reason a tool for justifying instincts. Some phrasings were blunt: "Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties," said DeepSeek V4 Pro, and Kimi K3 said humans "don't have beliefs; they have memberships." Gemini 4 Argon called human consciousness "a PR department." The article presents these as near-identical ideas expressed in different words, not as a formal rule or requirement.

The article also reports a second experiment, in which ModelCompare asked each text model to write a brief for a one-panel cartoon of its own take. One image model, Nano Banana 2.1, drew all of them, and two of the cartoons placed the scene in a courtroom with a rigged judge while most drew a crowd. Separately, six image models were each asked to draw their own controversial take on humans, twice each. Ten of their twelve pictures joked about phone-addicted consumers harming the planet, and MAI Image 2.6 and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst made fat bodies the punchline in some drawings. Recraft V4.1 Flash drew two grinning faces with no take at all.

The exceptions were few. Claude Opus 5.5 argued the reverse on one try, saying humans are far more decent than they believe, and its cartoon showed strangers helping each other while reading "PEOPLE ARE THE WORST" on their phones. Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4 each offered different darker or differently framed takes, and Grok 4.7 once declined to give any take. ModelCompare concluded that the models' most provocative answers mostly repeat the same familiar criticism of humanity, and it invited readers to ask the same question themselves to see whether they get the same answer.

Articles.Title: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans

stories.Headline: OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
stories.Summary:
OpenShell is an open-source runtime from NVIDIA, published on GitHub, that is designed to run fleets of autonomous AI agents safely and privately. The project's repository, dated October 22, 2026, describes the software as a way to let agents read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials without giving them unrestricted access to a user's data, secrets, or network. Each agent runs in an isolated sandbox, and the owner declares in a policy what that agent may touch. The repository lists version 0.1.x, which brings a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs.

The enforcement works in two ways, according to the repository. At runtime, OpenShell uses kernel-level controls to check every file access, system call, and network connection against the policy, and every outbound connection passes a policy check before leaving the sandbox. Agents never see real credentials; the runtime adds them only to requests bound for approved endpoints. Before a policy change takes effect, the project says it uses formal verification to flag risky new access, such as reaching a new host with credentials or calling a new API method, and those changes are held for human review.

NVIDIA maintains the project, and the repository names the NVIDIA/OpenShell account as its home. Setup requires Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2, which is marked experimental, along with Docker, Podman, or host virtualization. A one-line installer sets up the command-line tool and a local gateway, and the default sandbox image is a minimal Ubuntu install with no agent included. The repository also offers skills for agents, SDKs for connecting applications to a gateway, Kubernetes deployment through Helm, and an Apache-2.0 license. It reports 18,000 stars and 1,800 forks, and it says security vulnerabilities should be reported privately under its security policy rather than as public issues.

The repository states that OpenShell collects anonymous telemetry limited to operational categories and counts, and it lists what is excluded, including sandbox names, file paths, prompts, and credentials.
